title: 小失误，大麻烦：读 Tommy Tang 的生信常见错误清单
text:
2 min read
生信分析里的错误，大多并不高深：索引从错误的数字开始，没人记下用的是哪个基因组版本，或者 shell 命令里多了一个空格。这些错误容易犯、不容易发现，而且常常“静悄悄”：流程顺利跑完，结果看起来也挺合理。

title: 小失误，大麻烦：读 Tommy Tang 的生信常见错误清单
text:
1. 数数，比想象中难
不同文件格式的坐标系不同。 BED 是 0-based、左闭右开；GTF 和 GFF 是 1-based、两端闭合。染色体的第一个碱基，在 BED 里记为 0，在 GTF 里记为 1。格式转换时如果不调整起始位置，所有区域都会整体错开一个碱基，足以改变一个密码子，或错过剪接位点。
编程语言的计数起点不同。 Python 从 0 开始数，R 从 1 开始数。代码从一种语言改写到另一种，可能不报任何错，却总是取到相邻的那个元素。
染色体名不宜直接按普通文本排序。 普通文本排序会把 chr10 排在 chr2 前面，不符合通常按染色体编号排列的习惯。若要得到 chr1、chr2、…、chr10 的顺序，应使用自然排序；对于 BED 等区间文件，还需在每条染色体内按起始坐标排序。

好习惯：坐标每次跨越文件格式或编程语言时，先手动核对一个已知位置，比如某个熟悉基因的起点，再相信转换结果。

title: 小失误，大麻烦：读 Tommy Tang 的生信常见错误清单
section: 2. 数据和你以为的不一样
text:
2. 数据和你以为的不一样
基因组版本必须一致。 比对到 hg19 的 reads，如果套用 hg38 的注释来看，会落在外显子之外。参考序列、索引和注释文件都应来自同一个组装版本，最好也是同一个发布版本。
链方向很重要。 负链上的区域，提取序列前要先做反向互补。漏掉这一步，得到的序列格式完全正常，但内容是错的。
计数前，需要明确如何处理同时匹配多个基因的 reads。 基因之间可能相互重叠，甚至嵌套。统计 reads 前如果没想好共享区域怎么算，就可能漏掉某些特征，或把同一条 read 算两次。
换行符也有暗坑。 Windows 保存的文件用 \r\n 换行，Unix 工具期望的是 \n。最后一行如果没有换行符，简单的循环也可能把它漏掉。dos2unix 和一次 tail 检查就能避免很多麻烦。

好习惯：把基因组版本和注释版本写进文件名，也写进项目的 README。

title: 小失误，大麻烦：读 Tommy Tang 的生信常见错误清单
text:
3. Shell 错误
误删、误覆盖。

一个多余的空格，会把 rm *.fasta 变成 rm * .fasta，删掉整个文件夹里的文件。
> 会覆盖文件内容，>> 才是追加。用 > 往 ~/.bashrc 里写东西，原来的配置就没了。
在错误的目录里运行 rm *，删了就回不来。

本该交给程序的字符，被 shell 先处理了。

awk {print $2} 会出错，因为 shell 先展开了 $2 和花括号；应写成 awk '{print $2}'。
grep > file.fasta 不是在找序列标题，而是把输出重定向了；应写成 grep '>' file.fasta。
find . -name *.txt 中的通配符可能在 find 看到之前就被展开；模式要加引号。

忘了默认设置。

cut 默认按制表符切分，处理 CSV 需要加 -d,。
mkdir 要创建多层目录，需要加 -p。
rm 删除目录，需要加 -r。
用 cat 打开几个 GB 的 FASTQ 会刷满整个终端，head 或 less -S 更合适。
chmod 777 给所有人完全权限，通常 chmod u+x 就够了。


好习惯：用通配符删除前，先用同样的模式跑一次 ls。在 Bash 中，set -o noclobber 可以防止 > 覆盖已有文件。

section: 4. 流程上的错误，比代码错误影响更久
text:
4. 流程上的错误，比代码错误影响更久
尽量使用现成工具，避免重复造轮子。 读取 FASTQ、GenBank 或 BLAST 输出时，优先使用 Biopython、pysam、Bioconductor 等经过测试的库，省去自己编写读取代码的工作，也能减少遗漏特殊情况导致的错误。分析单细胞 RNA-seq 数据时，优先使用 Scanpy 或 Seurat 完成质控、降维和聚类，把精力放在研究问题上，无需自己从头编写代码。
正则表达式要测试。 用“应该匹配”和“不应该匹配”的例子各试一遍。
数据和代码都要有版本管理。 分析悄悄用了旧版输入，结果就很难复现。Git、Git LFS 或工作流管理工具能让输入一目了然。
记录决策，用对统计方法。 说不清怎么得到的结果，或依赖不合适的检验、不充分的随机化，还不能算发现。

title: 小失误，大麻烦：读 Tommy Tang 的生信常见错误清单
section: 5. 单细胞分析中的常见错误
text:
5. 单细胞分析中的常见错误
把细胞当作独立样本做差异表达。 比较健康与疾病两组、每组有多个样本时，常见做法是把每组所有细胞合在一起，在细胞水平做差异表达分析。但同一样本的细胞并不相互独立；成千上万个细胞会让 p 值被严重低估，产生大量假阳性。更稳妥的做法是伪批量（pseudobulk）分析：先把每个样本的细胞计数汇总，再以样本为单位比较。
过度解读 UMAP。 UMAP 是非线性降维方法，图上点与点、簇与簇之间的距离并没有明确的定量含义。它适合用来直观展示数据结构，不宜据此判断细胞群之间的远近关系。
默认批次校正是安全的。 批次校正和多数据集整合都建立在一定的假设之上，过度校正可能把真实的生物学差异一并抹去。一项比较了七种常用方法的研究发现，许多方法会在数据中引入可测量的人为改变，只有 Harmony 在所有测试中表现稳定，因此作者仅推荐 Harmony 用于 scRNA-seq 批次校正。Antonsson & Melsted, 2024

好习惯：差异表达以样本为单位；UMAP 只作可视化；批次校正后，检查已知的生物学差异是否仍然存在。

title: 小失误，大麻烦：读 Tommy Tang 的生信常见错误清单
text:
一张简短的检查表







在做这件事之前……
检查




转换坐标
0-based 还是 1-based？左闭右开还是两端闭合？


合并文件
基因组和注释版本一致吗？染色体命名一致吗（chr1 还是 1）？


提取序列
哪条链？


运行 rm、> 或 mv
目录对吗？模式先用 ls 确认过吗？


把代码传给 awk、grep 或 find
加引号了吗？


比较不同条件的表达
以样本为单位（pseudobulk）分析了吗？


分享结果
输入、版本和参数都记录了吗？



避免这些错误并不需要高深的知识，只需要多检查一下。这比重跑一遍分析便宜得多。

本文主要内容来自阅读 Tommy Tang 博客 Chatomics 上的文章《The Most Common Stupid Mistakes In Bioinformatics》。完整清单和更多资源请阅读原文。

title: nf-core/atacseq：用一把“分子剪刀”，找出基因组的开放区域
text:
2 min read
人体大多数有核体细胞拥有基本相同的DNA，却各有分工。一个直观的理解是：细胞不仅要有“说明书”，还要决定哪些页方便翻开，哪些页暂时收起来。
ATAC-seq 研究的，就是染色质的这种“可访问程度”。 而 nf-core/atacseq，则把测序后的数据整理成可以检查、比较和继续分析的结果。

title: nf-core/atacseq：用一把“分子剪刀”，找出基因组的开放区域
section: 1. 2013 年：把建库工具变成染色质探针
text:
1. 2013 年：把建库工具变成染色质探针
ATAC-seq 并不是第一个研究开放染色质的方法。在它出现之前，研究者已经使用 DNase-seq 等技术寻找这些区域。2013 年，Buenrostro 等人在 Nature Methods 发表 ATAC-seq，把一种更简便的实验思路带到了这个领域。[2]
它的巧思在于 Tn5 转座酶。这种酶能够切割 DNA，并把测序接头接到 DNA 上。在染色质中，DNA 的包装程度不同，Tn5 接近它的难易程度也不同：相对开放的区域更容易被插入接头。测序后，再把这些片段定位回基因组，就能推断哪些区域更容易被访问。[2]当然，标签多少也会受到实验条件和酶的偏好影响，因此测出来的是需要质控和统计解释的信号。
不同于 ChIP-seq 针对特定蛋白质与 DNA 的结合位置进行检测，ATAC-seq 和 DNase-seq主要用于描绘全基因组的染色质开放区域，无需针对特定蛋白质的抗体。相较于 DNase-seq，ATAC-seq利用Tn5转座酶同时完成 DNA 切割和测序接头插入，通常所需细胞更少、建库步骤更简洁，因此更适合样本量有限的研究。

title: nf-core/atacseq：用一把“分子剪刀”，找出基因组的开放区域
section: 2. 有趣的是，片段长度也在“讲故事”
text:
2. 有趣的是，片段长度也在“讲故事”
ATAC-seq 的信息不只来自“片段落在哪里”。DNA 会缠绕在组蛋白上形成核小体。测序得到的片段长度，因此也能反映这种包装结构：较短片段常与核小体缺失区域有关，较长片段可以包含一个或多个核小体对应的结构信息。[2]
所以，片段长度分布并不是报告里凑数的一张图。它把实验信号与染色质结构联系起来。这项技术后来继续改进。2017 年，Corces 等人提出 Omni-ATAC，改善信噪比，并拓展了对冷冻组织等样本的适用性。ATAC-seq 的发展，也是一段不断降低样本和实验门槛的历史。[3]

section: 3. 这条流程，最初竟然还与牛有关
text:
3. 这条流程，最初竟然还与牛有关
官方致谢记录：流程最初由 Harshil Patel 编写，后来由 Björn Langer 和 Jose Espinosa-Carrasco 在 BovReg 项目框架下迁移到 Nextflow DSL2。[1]
BovReg 研究牛基因组的功能调控，希望理解基因组及表观遗传差异如何与不同牛品种的性状联系起来。[4]
牛为什么也需要 ATAC-seq？因为知道 DNA序列，只是理解性状的一部分。要研究基因调控，还需要知道哪些区域在特定细胞或条件下可以被访问。这正是染色质可及性研究能够提供的线索。

title: nf-core/atacseq：用一把“分子剪刀”，找出基因组的开放区域
section: 4. Workflow：从 FASTQ 到开放染色质图谱
text:
4. Workflow：从 FASTQ 到开放染色质图谱
本文介绍的是 2.1.2 版本。下图来自官网：绿色线路表示文库合并后的分析，蓝色线路表示可选的跨生物学重复合并分析；方形节点表示必需步骤，圆形节点表示可选步骤。[1]



nf-core/atacseq 2.1.2 流程图


图 1. nf-core/atacseq 流程概览（2.1.2 版本）。来源：nf-core/atacseq。[1]

4.1 先清理 reads，再定位到基因组
原始 FASTQ 先经 FastQC 检查质量，再由 Trim Galore! 调用 Cutadapt 去除接头并进行质量修剪，随后再次质控。比对工具可选择 BWA（默认）、Bowtie2、STAR 或 Chromap。需要注意，2.1.2 中 Chromap 的双端数据仅处理到比对阶段，不进入后续分析。[1,5]
比对后，Picard 标记重复并合并同一生物学重复内的多批测序数据，再次标记重复后进行过滤。SAMtools、BEDTools、BAMTools 和 Pysam 共同去除线粒体来源、黑名单区域、重复及不可靠比对，并检查双端 reads 的配对情况。这一步减少技术噪声对峰识别的干扰。[1]


4.2 过滤之后，几条分析线路并行展开








分析任务
主要工具
作用




比对与文库质控
Picard、Preseq
检查比对质量，估计文库复杂度及继续测序的收益


信号轨道生成
BEDTools、bedGraphToBigWig
生成按每百万 mapped reads 缩放的 bigWig


信号富集检查
deepTools
查看转录起始位点、基因体及全基因组的信号分布


峰识别与注释
MACS2、HOMER
找到信号富集区域，注释其基因组位置及附近基因


共同区域构建与计数
BEDTools、featureCounts
整合 consensus peaks，在相同区域统计各样本 reads


样本比较与报告
R/DESeq2、ataqv、MultiQC、IGV
进行标准化、PCA 和聚类，汇总质控并支持轨道浏览



以上步骤对应官网流程图中的比对质控、富集分析、峰识别及报告分支。[1,5]


4.3 读图时，三个细节容易被忽略
第一，合并文库与合并生物学重复是两件事。 同一个重复分多次测序时，样本表中的 sample 和 replicate 相同，数据会在比对后合并。同一实验组的不同生物学重复，则使用相同 sample、不同 replicate。蓝色线路进一步合并这些重复以提高峰识别的覆盖度；即使使用这条线路生成的共识峰，计数仍来自各重复分别保留的比对数据，避免丢失重复之间的差异。[5]（样本表填写规则见官方使用文档。）
第二，峰的形状与共识峰的筛选都有默认设置。 该版本的 MACS2 默认调用 broad peaks，可用 --narrow_peak 改为 narrow peaks。Consensus peaks 默认来自各样本峰的并集，并不要求每个样本都出现；可通过 --min_reps_consensus 提高重复支持要求。[5]
第三，流程里的DESeq2会生成PCA和聚类图，帮助查看样本是否相似；要判断处理组与对照组哪些区域有显著差异，还需要按实验分组设置统计分析。[5]

text:
5. nf-core/atacseq 把数据变成了什么？
实验负责留下“标签”，分析流程负责解释标签的位置和分布。
2.1.2 版本将原始测序质控、接头去除、比对、过滤、峰识别和报告生成组织成 Nextflow 工作流，并使用容器管理软件环境。[1]
其中，peak（峰）可以理解为测序信号显著富集的一段基因组区域。
阅读结果时，可以先抓住三个问题：[5]

对应结果

MultiQC、ataqv 及相关质控指标


哪些区域存在可及性信号？
MACS2 peaks、bigWig 信号轨道


不同样本能否在同一套区域上比较？
consensus peaks、区域计数矩阵、PCA 和聚类

title: nf-core/atacseq：用一把“分子剪刀”，找出基因组的开放区域
section: 6. 看到了开放区域，然后呢？
text:
6. 看到了开放区域，然后呢？
ATAC-seq 的吸引力在于它给基因组增加了一个新的观察角度：除了序列本身，还能观察细胞怎样开放和包装这些序列。
nf-core/atacseq 则把这个观察过程落实为可复用的分析步骤。读懂结果之后，真正有意思的工作才开始：把开放区域、基因表达和实验条件连接起来，形成可以检验的生物学解释。

title: nf-core/sarek：从 DNA 测序到“基因组找不同”
section: 名字像景点，干的是科研的活
text:
名字像景点，干的是科研的活
Sarek 听起来像某个算法的缩写，其实它和瑞典北部一座同名国家公园有关。开发者在介绍流程时还展示过公园的风景，早期版本也用过 Ruotes、Skårki 等名字。别人发新版本：v2.1、v2.2；它发新版本，顺便给你上一小节瑞典地理课。出处见开发者的 2020 年介绍。
不过，这个项目的出身很务实：最初由瑞典 SciLifeLab 旗下的 NGI 和 NBIS 团队开发，得到瑞典儿童肿瘤生物样本库的支持。后来，德国 QBiC 的开发者也加入了进来，并与其他贡献者一起推动后续开发和 Nextflow DSL2 重构。[1]
测完一个人的 DNA，拿到的不是一份完整的基因组说明书，而是海量短小的序列片段。把这些碎片放回正确位置，再找出哪些字母换了、哪些段落删了、哪些章节多了几份，就是变异分析的基本任务。
它要解决的麻烦，做过分析的人应该不陌生：数据终于拿到了，接下来却要安装一串软件、处理不同文件格式，再祈祷换台服务器后还能跑。测序仪已经下班，分析的人还在和环境报错加班。Sarek 把这些步骤组织成可重复运行的工作流，让研究者少花些时间接管道，多花些时间看结果。
nf-core/sarek 把这件事串成了一条自动化流程：预处理 → 变异检测 → 注释 → 质量报告。它既能分析个体原本携带的生殖系变异，也能寻找肿瘤等组织后来产生的体细胞变异。[1]

text:
2. 为什么变异分析这么重要？
如果把基因组比作一本说明书，RNA 表达分析关注的是“哪些章节正在被阅读、读了多少”；DNA 变异分析关注的是“说明书的内容发生了什么变化”。
这些变化与许多研究问题直接相关：

遗传病研究：某个基因的变异，是否可能影响蛋白质功能？
癌症研究：肿瘤新增了哪些突变？哪些区域发生扩增或缺失？
群体遗传研究：不同个体携带哪些差异？这些差异与性状有什么关系？

因此，变异检测是 DNA 测序分析中的基础环节。但“与参考基因组不同”不等于“有害”：大量变异只是正常的个体差异。找到变异后，还需要注释、筛选和进一步解释。

section: 5. 为什么分 germline 和 somatic 两条路线？
text:
5. 为什么分 germline 和 somatic 两条路线？
Germline（生殖系）分析：这个人原本携带哪些变异？这些变异通常存在于几乎所有细胞中，可以来自父母，也可以是新发变异。
Somatic（体细胞）分析：某些细胞后来新增了哪些变异？在癌症研究中，常用同一患者的肿瘤与配对正常样本比较，帮助区分原有遗传背景和肿瘤新增变化。
检测难度也不同。在正常二倍体、没有拷贝数变化的常染色体区域，germline 杂合变异通常有约 50% 的 reads 支持变异。肿瘤样本则混合了正常细胞、肿瘤细胞和不同肿瘤亚群，真实 somatic 变异可能只得到少量 reads 的支持。
例如，假设 20% 的细胞带有一个杂合突变，其余细胞没有，而且没有拷贝数变化，那么预期的变异等位基因比例（VAF）约为：
\[
\mathrm{VAF} \approx 20\% \times \frac{1}{2} = 10\%
\]
软件必须判断：这 10% 是真实突变，还是测序或比对错误？因此，两条路线需要不同的统计模型和过滤逻辑。GATK 的 HaplotypeCaller 主要用于 germline 检测，Mutect2 则用于 somatic 检测。[1]

title: nf-core/sarek：从 DNA 测序到“基因组找不同”
text:
6. 步骤

第一步：预处理——先把证据整理好
检查 reads 的质量，按需去除接头，把序列比对到参考基因组，标记重复 reads，并进行适用的碱基质量校正。[1]
这里应避免“假证据”：如果一条 DNA 片段被反复扩增，这些拷贝不应被当成许多独立分子在支持同一个突变；一条 read 放错位置，也可能制造出并不存在的差异。


第二步：变异检测——选择合适的工具
根据 germline 或 somatic 研究目标，以及需要寻找的变异类型，选择相应 caller。比如，germline 小变异可以使用 HaplotypeCaller 或 DeepVariant，somatic 小变异可以使用 Mutect2，结构变异则交给 Manta 等工具。[1]


第三步：注释——从坐标变成生物学问题
一个变异坐标本身并不容易理解。VEP、SnpEff 等工具会补充信息：它落在哪个基因、哪个转录本？是否改变氨基酸？是否可能影响剪接？[1]
这一步把“某个位置 A 变成 G”转化为“这个变化可能影响某个蛋白质”。


第四步：报告——检查结果，也检查质量
运行结束后，通常得到处理后的比对文件、VCF 变异文件，以及所选工具对应的结果。CNV、MSI 等模块还会产生各自的表格或图形报告。
MultiQC 汇总质量指标，帮助查看测序覆盖度、比对情况和重复率等。[1]






Tip



Execution report：记录整个 Nextflow 流程的执行情况，告诉你各步骤是否成功，以及耗时和资源消耗。

title: scRNA-seq：Cell Ranger 与 Simpleaf 路线的 barcode 分歧
text:
为什么做这个
Nextflow 管理并记录分析过程，nf-core/scrnaseq 提供单细胞RNA的多条标准化处理路线。我想知道：同一批测序数据，为什么不同路线保留的细胞不完全相同？ 多出的 barcode 是真实细胞、背景 RNA，还是低质量液滴？它们会不会改变生物学结论？

title: scRNA-seq：Cell Ranger 与 Simpleaf 路线的 barcode 分歧
text:
方法
数据为 10x 公开的 PBMC 1k v3，流程为 nf-core/scrnaseq 4.2.0。两边使用同一批 FASTQ、GRCh38-2024-A 参考：Cell Ranger 用预建索引，Simpleaf 用包内 FASTA/GTF 建索引。
版本为 Cell Ranger 10.0.0、Simpleaf 0.19.5、QCatch 0.2.12。 这里比较的是 Cell Ranger 与 Simpleaf＋QCatch：Simpleaf 负责计数，QCatch 负责后续细胞识别。
上游在 AWS r6i.4xlarge（16 vCPU、128 GiB）运行，采用 CloudFormation 自动安装、分析、上传结果后自动终止实例。成功的一次全程 84 分钟；账单约 $2.05，含 3 次失败尝试，成功的那次约 $1.41。本样本的下游比较在 8 GB Mac 个人电脑上完成。

# 1221 0 7

这 7 个 barcode 都集中在细胞与背景的过渡区域。



Barcode 排名及拐点放大：绿色标记为仅 Simpleaf＋QCatch 保留的 7 个 barcode


横轴为 UMI 排名，纵轴为 UMI 数。右图空心圆为 Cell Ranger，菱形为 Simpleaf；连线对应同一 barcode。500 UMI 是本次实现的检验门槛，不是所有 EmptyDrops 分析的固定值。
按交集／并集计算，细胞集合一致率为 99.4%。共同细胞中，每个细胞总 UMI 的 Spearman 相关系数为 0.9997，Simpleaf 平均计数约高 5%。整体高度一致，但小差异能改变边界 barcode 的去留。
还要注意：图中的两份“原始矩阵”分别包含 329,735 和 72,612 个 barcode。它们的上游保留范围不同，不能当成完全相同的液滴全集。

3. 是细胞识别算法不同，还是输入计数不同？
我用同一套 QCatch 代码和参数，以 OrdMag＋EmptyDrops 框架重新识别两份矩阵。
# QCatch 内部接口节选；m 为 CountMatrix，cc 为细胞识别模块。

initial = cc.initial_filtering_OrdMag(m, "10X_3p_v3", None)
res = cc.find_nonambient_barcodes(m, initial, "10X_3p_v3", None)
called = {b.decode() for b in initial} | set(res.eval_bcs[res.is_nonambient])
Cell Ranger 矩阵仍得到 1,221 个，Simpleaf 矩阵仍得到 1,228 个，与原结果逐个一致。改变随机种子和模拟次数后，本次分歧也未消失。
同一识别实现仍有分歧，接下来应查输入矩阵。 但输入差异包括计数和背景 barcode 范围，不能只归因于某个单一因素。

3 个跨过了 500 UMI 门槛
1、5、6 号在 Cell Ranger 矩阵中低于 500 UMI，未进入这一步的非背景检验；在 Simpleaf 矩阵中则超过门槛。额外计数中，DHFR 占了显著一部分。

重复序列是 DHFR 异常计数的线索。 两条路线的参考目标和比对／分配规则不同，可能导致这些 reads 的归属不同。未逐条核对 Simpleaf 的 read 分配，因此机制仍是推断，chr8 lncRNA 也不能凭类比认定原因。
注意：Cell Ranger 会根据基因归属调整 MAPQ，不能简化为“只计唯一基因组比对”。MAPQ＝255 不必然代表原始 STAR 比对只有一个位置。10x BAM 标签说明

section: 最后：这 7 个值得在意吗？
text:
最后：这 7 个值得在意吗？
对细胞类型比例：几乎没有影响。 我固定计数、聚类和注释，只改变细胞集。多出的 7 个分属 4 类：血小板 2 个、cDC 2 个、FCGR3A 单核 1 个、低质量 2 个。其余细胞类型的细胞数完全没变，只是分母从 1,221 变成 1,228，比例被稀释，最多 0.16 个百分点。按常见 QC（≥ 200 个基因、线粒体 ≤ 20%）过滤后，差异只剩 3 个细胞：2 个 cDC、1 个 FCGR3A 单核。
这个变化有多小？我在同一流程里只改聚类随机种子，或只换计数矩阵，作为对照：



只改变一个因素时，各类细胞比例的最大变化


蓝：只换细胞集；橙：只换聚类随机种子（0–4）；绿：只换计数矩阵（Cell Ranger 或 Simpleaf）。
细胞集带来的变化最多 0.16 个百分点；随机种子或计数矩阵却能让单核、NK／CD8 T 的比例变化 6–10 个百分点。后两项来自我这套简单的聚类／注释方法，不能推广为工具差异。比起这 7 个 barcode，注释对分析设置的敏感性更值得检查。
对小细胞群的 marker：有影响，但有限。 cDC 只有 16 个细胞，多 2 个就是 +12.5%。



cDC marker 的表达比例与校正后 p 值


CST3、FCER1A、CLEC10A 的结论不变。CD1C 变弱：表达比例从 63% 降到 56%，校正后 p 值从 0.012 升到 0.034，因为新增的 2 个细胞不表达 CD1C。另外，QC 后两边是同一批 15 个血小板，PPBP 的 marker 排名却从第 13 变为第 1，因为前列基因分数接近。看 marker，要看表达比例、效应大小和统计证据，不能只看排名。

title: scRNA-seq：Cell Ranger 与 Simpleaf 路线的 barcode 分歧
text:
结论
同一批 FASTQ，Cell Ranger 保留 1,221 个细胞，Simpleaf＋QCatch 保留 1,228 个，前者全部包含在后者中。我追查了多出的 7 个 barcode：3 个因额外计数跨过 UMI 门槛，DHFR 内含子重复序列是其中的重要线索；另外 4 个处于统计阈值附近。只改变细胞集时，细胞类型比例最多变化 0.16 个百分点。这 7 个对整体细胞类型比例影响很小，但少数基因与固定阈值足以改变去留。两次比较仅使用了一份 PBMC 样本；两种流程在其他数据中是否同样接近，还需要进一步验证。

text: 6 min read

title: Matrix Operations and Linear Algebra
section: 1. Tensors have a funny name. Matrices are fashionable, too.
text:
1. Tensors have a funny name. Matrices are fashionable, too.
The Chinese word for tensor is 张量, pronounced zhāng liàng. My surname is also Zhang. Every time I look at the word, I wonder whether I should adopt it as my name. That would give me a connection to deep learning before I even wrote any code.
Just a small joke from someone named Zhang.
“Matrix” has its own appeal. A name like “Matrix Technology” sounds ready for an office full of algorithms. “Magic square” adds a mathematical twist: a square arrangement of numbers whose rows, columns, and two main diagonals have equal sums.
But a matrix is more than a fashionable name. Open an expression table, and you are probably already looking at one.








Name
A practical picture
Example




Scalar
One number
Sequencing depth for one sample


Vector
A sequence of numbers
One gene’s expression across samples


Matrix
Numbers arranged in rows and columns
Genes × samples


Tensor
An array that can have more axes
Batch × sequence positions × features



Deep learning libraries commonly call these arrays tensors. Mathematical tensors have a more precise definition, but array shape is a useful starting point here. The number of axes should not be confused with matrix rank.

title: Matrix Operations and Linear Algebra
section: 2. Much of bioinformatics starts with a matrix
text:
2. Much of bioinformatics starts with a matrix
Different experiments often give us similarly structured tables:








Data
Common rows × columns
Meaning of an entry




Bulk RNA-seq
Genes × samples
Assigned read or fragment counts, sometimes estimated counts


Single-cell RNA-seq
Genes × cells
Deduplicated UMI counts in common droplet-based UMI assays


ChIP-seq
Peaks × samples
Reads or fragments counted within a peak


Drug response
Drugs × samples
IC50 or another sensitivity measure



A single-cell count need not be a raw read count. For example, Cell Ranger gene-expression matrices record UMI counts: several reads can correspond to one counted molecule.
Orientation varies, too. Some tools store cells × genes. Before calculating anything, ask: What does a row represent? What does a column represent? What does an entry measure?
For IC50, check units, missingness, and measurement limits. Under comparable assay conditions, a lower value generally means a lower concentration is needed for half-maximal inhibition. Values from different conditions should not be pooled uncritically.



A gene-by-sample matrix and grouped sums


Figure 1. Four synthetic genes and three samples. Matrix multiplication combines S1 and S2 into group A and assigns S3 to group B.

2.1 Transpose: turn the table around
Let C have four gene rows and three sample columns:
import numpy as np

C = np.array([
    [10, 20, 30],
    [ 0,  5, 10],
    [ 3,  6,  9],
    [ 8,  4,  0],
])
print(C.shape)    # (4, 3): genes × samples
print(C.T.shape)  # (3, 4): samples × genes
Transposition swaps the axes without changing the values. It is useful when a machine learning tool expects samples in rows and features in columns.


2.2 Matrix multiplication: match, multiply, and add
For A with shape m × k and B with shape k × n:
\[
(AB)_{ij}=\sum_{r=1}^{k}A_{ir}B_{rj},\qquad AB\text{ has shape }m\times n.
\]
Start with one output entry: take a row from the left matrix and a column from the right, multiply matching entries, then add them.
To sum S1 and S2 into group A while leaving S3 in group B:
P = np.array([
    [1, 0],  # S1 → A
    [1, 0],  # S2 → A
    [0, 1],  # S3 → B
])
group_counts = C @ P
print(group_counts)
# [[30 30]
#  [ 5 10]
#  [ 9  9]
#  [12  0]]
The shapes are (4, 3) @ (3, 2) → (4, 2). The three-sample axis is summed over, leaving four genes and two groups.
This demonstrates summation, not differential expression. Do not casually pool biological replicates: sequencing depth and the number of samples affect group totals. Single-cell pseudobulk commonly aggregates separately by biological sample and cell type to preserve replication.


2.3 * and @ are different operations
In NumPy, * multiplies entries element by element, while @ performs matrix multiplication. The official documentation describes its shape rules.
A = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
B = np.array([[5, 6], [7, 8]])
print(A * B)  # [[ 5, 12], [21, 32]]
print(A @ B)  # [[19, 22], [43, 50]]
Both lines run. They answer different questions. That little symbol deserves a second look when reading code.


2.4 PCA: look along a different set of directions
Matrices can describe directions in which to examine data. PCA finds directions of large variation and projects samples onto them.
Here is a small example using singular value decomposition (SVD):
E = np.log1p(C.T.astype(float))       # samples × genes
E_centered = E - E.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(E_centered, full_matrices=False)
scores = E_centered @ Vt[:2].T
print(scores.shape)                 # (3, 2)
Vt[:2].T supplies two directions; scores contains the coordinates of three samples along them. The NumPy SVD documentation explains the factorization and reconstruction.
Direct log1p is only a teaching shortcut here. Real RNA-seq PCA requires appropriate depth handling and transformation, plus a decision about gene scaling. Large variation may reflect disease, batch, or something else; PCA does not decide that for us.

title: Matrix Operations and Linear Algebra
section: 3. Deep learning also runs on matrix operations
text:
3. Deep learning also runs on matrix operations
A fully connected layer can be written as:
\[H=f(XW+b).\]
X holds inputs, W holds learned weights, b is a bias, and f is an activation function. Each output feature starts as a weighted sum of input features.



Matrix shapes in a fully connected layer


Figure 2. Five samples with four features pass through a 4 × 3 weight matrix, producing three output features per sample. Bias is added to each row.
X = np.ones((5, 4))
W = np.ones((4, 3))
b = np.zeros(3)
H = np.maximum(0, X @ W + b)  # ReLU
print(H.shape)               # (5, 3)
Without nonlinear activation, several layers of multiplication and bias can still be combined into one affine transformation. More layers alone do not automatically yield a richer function.
For a batch of sequences, the input might be batch × tokens × features. The array now has three axes, but multiplication still often operates on the last two. Calling it a tensor does not make familiar arithmetic disappear.

title: Matrix Operations and Linear Algebra
text:
4. Two multiplications inside Transformer attention
Attention can be approached through two questions:

How much information should each position take from the others?
How should that information be combined?

The original Transformer paper defines scaled dot-product attention as:
\[\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V.\]
Different weight matrices map the input to Q, K, and V. Q @ K.T produces scores between positions. Row-wise softmax turns them into weights summing to one. Those weights then combine the rows of V.
Here is one unmasked attention head with random, untrained weights:
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
X = rng.normal(size=(3, 4))    # three positions, four features each
Wq = rng.normal(size=(4, 2))
Wk = rng.normal(size=(4, 2))
Wv = rng.normal(size=(4, 2))
Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv

scores_attention = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(Q.shape[1])
z = scores_attention - scores_attention.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
A = np.exp(z)
A /= A.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
Y = A @ V
print(A.shape, Y.shape)       # (3, 3) (3, 2)
Subtracting each row’s maximum improves numerical stability without changing softmax. A row of A describes how one position distributes its weights; Y contains the combined representations.



Attention weights computed by the example


Figure 3. Computed attention weights from the fixed-seed example above; every row sums to one. These are random weights, not results from a trained language model.
A complete Transformer also uses multiple heads, position information, residual connections, normalization, and feed-forward networks. Text generation usually requires a causal mask so a position cannot read future positions. The example shows only one core operation.
From grouped expression sums to PCA projection and attention, matrix multiplication keeps turning one collection of numbers into another. The important questions remain: what do the axes mean, where did the weights come from, and what does the output help us understand?
The full matrix_demo.py requires NumPy:
python3 examples/matrix_demo.py
Examples were run with NumPy 2.3.5. Checks cover grouped sums, SVD reconstruction, and attention row sums. All data are constructed for teaching, not real sequencing observations.

title: RNA-seq plots by R
text:
2 min read

Making the same five RNA-seq figures from scratch, every single project, for the hundredth time? Yeah, me too. So I finally sat down and turned the whole mess into one R script that spits out a publication-ready panel figure and doesn’t ask me a single follow-up question.

Five panels, one dataset, no copy-pasted ggplot incantations: A PCA with group ellipses and batch shapes, B a sample correlation heatmap that clusters itself, C a volcano plot that actually labels the genes worth knowing about, D a two-module expression heatmap with side bar charts for flair, and E violin plots for the genes everyone’s going to ask about anyway. Patchwork glues them into one A–E composite so nobody has to eyeball five separate PNGs and pretend they form a coherent story.
The example data is 800 simulated genes across 24 samples — two groups, two batches. Swap in your own expression.csv, samples.csv, and differential_expression.csv and the whole pipeline runs on real numbers instead.
Running it is embarrassingly simple:
install.packages(c('ggplot2', 'ggrepel', 'patchwork', 'ragg', 'svglite', 'circlize'),
                 repos = 'https://cloud.r-project.org')
install.packages('BiocManager')
BiocManager::install('ComplexHeatmap', ask = FALSE, update = FALSE)

source('run.R')
That’s it. No notebook archaeology, no “wait, which chunk made the heatmap again.” Every plot function also works standalone if you just want one panel for a talk instead of the whole gallery.

title: Genome plots by R
text:
2 min read

Need a circos plot, a chromosome map, and a zoomed-in regional view, and you’d rather not spend an afternoon fighting circlize margins again? Same idea as last time, same afternoon saved.

Four views, one coordinate system, no re-deriving Mb math at 2am: A a circular genome overview stacking gene density, GC and signal tracks with interval links through the middle, B a chromosome map marking target genes and highlighted regions, C the same three tracks laid out linearly per chromosome for when circles aren’t the point, and D a regional zoom on one window with strand-aware gene arrows. Patchwork stitches the global and regional views into one composite so the detail panel doesn’t float around looking lost.
The genome is entirely made up — six fictional chromosomes, about 545 one-megabase bins, 288 gene spans. It exists to make the coordinate math behave, not to represent anything you’d find in Ensembl. Point it at your own chromosomes.csv, bins.csv, genes.csv, regions.csv and links.csv and it draws your actual genome instead.
The one thing this project is pedantic about: coordinates are 1-based and closed, both ends included. Coming from a BED file? Add 1 to the start, leave the end alone. Get that wrong once and every track is off by a base — see Ming “Tommy” Tang’s post on exactly this mistake: Most common mistake for bioinformatics.
Running it:
install.packages(c('ggplot2', 'patchwork', 'circlize', 'gridGraphics',
                   'ggrepel', 'ragg', 'svglite'), repos = 'https://cloud.r-project.org')

source('run.R')
Five figures and one composite land in figures/, PNG and SVG both. Every plotting function works on its own too, if all you need today is the circle.

title: Workflow Management in Bioinformatics and Deep Learning
text: 5 min read

title: Workflow Management in Bioinformatics and Deep Learning
text:
Worlds Apart in Workflow Management
In bioinformatics, analyzing a single sample often involves a dozen or even several dozen independent command-line tools developed by different laboratories: BWA for alignment, samtools for sorting, GATK for variant calling, and FastQC for quality control, for example. Written in languages ranging from C and C++ to Python and Perl, these tools also work with a variety of file formats, including FASTQ, SAM/BAM, and VCF. For large analyses that must be reproducible, workflow engines such as Nextflow and Snakemake often bring these separate tools together through scripts and containers (Docker or Singularity). One reason is that bioinformatics software is developed and maintained by research groups large and small all over the world.


 

By contrast, the model-training stage of deep learning is usually more cohesive. Frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow provide a relatively unified programming environment: data loading, the forward pass, loss computation, backpropagation, and optimizer updates can all happen in the same codebase. There is no need to write an intermediate file and invoke a separate external program at every step. One reason is that PyTorch and TensorFlow are developed and maintained by large companies such as Meta and Google.
End-to-end programmability: Data loading (DataLoader), the model’s forward pass (Forward), loss computation (Loss), backpropagation (Backward), and optimizer updates (Optimizer) can flow through a single Python script or framework object, without repeatedly writing intermediate files and calling standalone external binaries.
A more cohesive model-training workflow: Bioinformatics pipelines can branch into hundreds or thousands of tool combinations depending on the sequencing platform, reference genome version, and analytical goal (RNA-seq versus ChIP-seq). Deep-learning code, meanwhile, is highly modular: changing a model architecture or loss function may take only a few lines of Python, without requiring Nextflow to orchestrate separate applications.

What Does Standardization Look Like in Deep Learning?
Although deep learning does not always need a workflow engine to connect a collection of standalone tools, it faces its own challenges in experiment management, hyperparameter search, model deployment, and pipeline reproducibility. Different layers of standardization have therefore emerged:
Lifecycle and experiment tracking (in the spirit of nf-core)

MLflow: Manages the machine-learning lifecycle by recording training parameters, code versions, evaluation metrics, and model weights so that experiments can be reproduced.
Weights & Biases (W&B): A widely used tool in industry and academia for visualizing and tracking experiments, and for comparing performance across training runs.

Production-scale pipeline orchestration (the closest parallel to a workflow engine)

Kubeflow: A Kubernetes-based machine-learning toolkit that can orchestrate data preprocessing, distributed training, model validation, and deployment as a directed acyclic graph (DAG).
TFX (TensorFlow Extended): A production-grade ML platform developed by Google for standardized pipelines covering large-scale data validation, training, and inference.

Easy reuse and reproducibility (a research-side analogue to nf-core)

Hugging Face Transformers / Timm: In areas such as computer vision and natural language processing, these libraries serve as collections of standard building blocks. Instead of writing every training loop and low-level operation from scratch, you can use packaged models and datasets to assemble a complete workflow.

title: Workflow Management in Bioinformatics and Deep Learning
section: One Workflow to Rule Them All?
text:
One Workflow to Rule Them All?







To be fair, standards start with good intentions. Each promises to bring order to a fragmented field. It is a little like the ambition behind Tolkien’s One Ring: one ring to rule them all. Yet every new standard can become another little kingdom, complete with its own rules and followers. Each would like developers to enter its orbit, but reality is less accommodating. When one standard disappoints, another appears. The race to standardize can end in a proliferation of standards. Workflow languages alone now include Snakemake, Nextflow, CWL, and WDL.

title: Workflow Management in Bioinformatics and Deep Learning
text:
Back to Basics

What is the most basic language for invoking bioinformatics tools? The shell on Linux and other Unix-like systems – most often Bash.
Why? Because we commonly use the shell to call bioinformatics software on a server. Whatever framework sits above it, an analysis ultimately comes down to concrete tasks: which files go in, which commands run, which parameters are used, and which results come out. That points to two principles for building bioinformatics workflows:

For a small, one-off analysis, a shell script may be all you need.
As the workflow grows more complex, Python can handle the logic, or Nextflow or Snakemake can manage the tasks. In either case, the commands each task actually runs and the logs it produces should be easy to inspect.

These principles also help us judge a workflow framework. A good one manages complexity while keeping what actually runs transparent.

title: My Story
text:
5 min read


My family ran a small village shop when I was a child. Buying and selling kept us going, and my parents taught me numbers and arithmetic early. By age three, I was behind the counter. A customer would hand me money and ask for candy; I would count it out, pack it up, work out the price, and return every last bit of change. I rarely made a mistake. The neighbors loved to tease me about it, and our little shop was often full of laughter.
Then my father’s job took us to another town. One curious neighbor liked to borrow me to mind her shop. People would gather just to watch a child balance the books to the last cent. That early feel for numbers followed me to school. I often earned full marks in math, and I won math competition prizes without extra tutoring or endless practice sheets. I assumed I would keep following that path.
Life, of course, had other plans. When it was time to choose a university major, the claim that “the 21st century belongs to life sciences” won me over. I chose life sciences without hesitation. I was hardly alone: from 1999 to 2007, many of China’s top entrance exam scorers made the same choice. Once classes began, though, the dream met reality. There were endless facts about plants, animals, and anatomy to memorize. I drifted through my days, unsure how to study and even less sure where I belonged. The field I had entered with such hope became what people called a major with bleak prospects. As admission scores fell year after year, I felt the distance between the promise and the reality. That was my first hurdle: I had plenty of passion, but nowhere to put it.
Graduate school at the Chinese Academy of Sciences came as genomics was taking off. My adviser worked in cell biology, but a series of turns led me into evolutionary genomics and then bioinformatics. There, at last, I found my way back to the quantitative thinking I had loved as a child. I learned that an early interest can shape a lifetime of work.
The next wave brought next generation sequencing, whole genome sequencing, RNA sequencing, and proteomics. I rode that wave. I published more than 50 papers in international journals, received national awards and research funding, and became a full professor while still relatively young. Colleagues told me I could simply enjoy what I had built until retirement. For a while, I almost did. But a problem was growing beneath the calm: traditional statistics struggled with the flood of biological data. Breakthroughs became harder to find, and publishing became harder too. I could see the road ahead but could barely move along it. That was my second hurdle: from a position others envied, I could see the ceiling above me.
Then AI began changing every field, including mine. My students showed me the opening. When your students know more than you do about a new subject, the best thing a teacher can do is encourage them and let them pull you forward. I am grateful for those remarkable young people. Our shared enthusiasm and humor have kept us close, and their kind words online still mean a great deal to me. Even so, entering AI from scratch was frightening. I had to rebuild my knowledge from the ground up. I started arriving at the office at five in the morning and leaving at eleven at night, as if I were back in high school preparing for exams. Some nights, after struggling through one more difficult concept, I asked myself whether all this effort at my age was worth it. That was my third hurdle.
Thankfully, the work paid off. We made the transition. Take protein research: we used to extract sequence features by hand. That worked at first, but eventually we hit a wall. With protein language models such as ESM2, a single sequence can yield 5,120 features and capture relationships between distant parts of a protein. This can make protein function predictions more accurate and interpretable, and help models work across species. In synthetic biology, it can also address a pressing industrial need: finding enzymes with better catalytic performance.
I went on to study data science, machine learning, deep learning, and cloud computing systematically. I once earned a top global score on DataCamp, honed my skills in Kaggle competitions, and explored targeted therapy with a Harvard professor. Over time, I learned to connect mathematics, linear algebra, statistics, computer science, software and data engineering, cloud computing, machine learning, bioinformatics, computational biology, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, structural biology, immunology, precision oncology, and pharmacology. The longer I study them, the more connections I see. Those connections are what I hope to share in this blog.
I am grateful to live in a time when knowledge is easier to reach than ever. Anyone willing to put in the work can enter a new field.
Growing older is inevitable. Losing your curiosity is not. At any stage of life, the desire to learn can open the door to a new beginning.

title: Nextflow: Reproducible Bioinformatics at Scale
text:
2 min read


In modern computational biology, reproducibility is no longer a bonus. It is the standard.
Running an RNA-seq pipeline once is no longer the hard part. The real test is running it again—across hundreds of samples, different collaborators, HPC clusters, and the cloud—and getting results you can trust every time.
That is why Nextflow is becoming an essential skill alongside R and Python. A pipeline that works only on your laptop is a fragile experiment. A workflow that others can run and reproduce is research they can build on.
Achieving reproducible workflows through Docker, Singularity, and Conda.
Imagine being able to answer “yes” to all three questions:

Can I process 500 RNA-seq samples with the same workflow?
Can collaborators run it on an HPC cluster, AWS, or Azure?
If a sample fails halfway through, can I resume the analysis without starting over?

The infographic shows a typical RNA-seq pipeline, but the same workflow approach applies to:

Single-cell RNA-seq (Cell Ranger → Scanpy or Seurat)
ChIP-seq (Bowtie2 → MACS3 peak calling)
WGS/WES variant calling (BWA → GATK → VEP)
Shotgun metagenomics (fastp → MEGAHIT assembly → MetaBAT2 binning)
DNA methylation sequencing (Bismark alignment → methylation calling)

Want to explore real Nextflow workflows? Start here:

nf-core Pipelines — A community collection of tested pipelines covering RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, methylation analysis, metagenomics, and more.
Awesome Nextflow — A curated collection of pipelines, examples, modules, and learning resources.

title: What If You want Customize an nf-core Pipeline?
text:
4 min read
Take nf-core/rnaseq as an example: if your research question calls for a different analysis path, where should you make the change?

title: What If You want Customize an nf-core Pipeline?
section: 1. How Many Steps Are in nf-core/rnaseq?
text:
1. How Many Steps Are in nf-core/rnaseq?
The official overview lists 16 categories of tasks, but they are not 16 steps that every run executes in sequence. Broadly, the pipeline can merge FASTQ files and infer library strandedness; run FastQC; extract UMIs and trim reads; optionally remove contaminants and rRNA; align reads and quantify expression; process BAM files; generate expression and coverage outputs; and compile QC results in MultiQC. Several alignment and quantification routes are available, so the tasks that actually run depend on your input and settings. nf-core/rnaseq produces an expression matrix; for downstream differential expression analysis, you can use nf-core/differentialabundance.

title: What If You want Customize an nf-core Pipeline?
text:
2. Which Files Matter for Customization?
Before making changes, distinguish these four file types.










File type
What it controls
What the pipeline or community provides
What you typically supply
How they relate




Nextflow scripts (.nf)
Analysis steps: which tools run, how data moves, and which commands are executed
main.nf is the entry point; workflows/*.nf connects steps and data; modules/…/main.nf defines individual steps and commands
Usually no .nf edits
Source code determines what runs and how steps connect


Parameter files
Analysis choices: input, outdir, genome, etc.
nextflow_schema.json describes parameters; nextflow.config or .nf files provide some defaults
params.yaml or params.json via -params-file; for a few values, command-line options such as –input
Your values replace the corresponding defaults


Configuration files
Execution settings: CPUs, memory, containers, Slurm, etc.
Pipeline nextflow.config and conf/*.config; shared cluster profiles such as uppmax.config (loaded with -profile uppmax)
custom.config when needed, passed with -c custom.config
Override only the settings you need to change


Samplesheet
The sample list
Pipeline documentation specifies CSV columns and format
samplesheet.csv
List your samples and FASTQ file paths

title: What If You want Customize an nf-core Pipeline?
section: 3. Switch Trimming Tools with a Command-Line Parameter
text:
3. Switch Trimming Tools with a Command-Line Parameter
Suppose you want to replace the default Trim Galore! trimmer with fastp. The pipeline already supports –trimmer fastp, so add that option to your command:
nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq -r 3.27.0 \
  --input samplesheet.csv \
  --fasta genome.fa \
  --gtf annotation.gtf \
  --trimmer fastp \
  --outdir results_fastp \
  -profile docker
If your parameter file also says trimmer: trimgalore, the command-line option –trimmer fastp takes precedence. To compare the tools fairly, keep the samples, reference files, and pipeline version fixed; save outputs separately; then compare retained reads, FastQC/MultiQC metrics, and downstream alignment results.

title: What If You want Customize an nf-core Pipeline?
text:
4. Save Analysis Choices in params.yaml
Suppose you want to keep STAR as the aligner but switch quantification from the default STAR → Salmon route to STAR → RSEM. Put the choices in params.yaml:
input: samplesheet.csv
fasta: genome.fa
gtf: annotation.gtf
outdir: results_rsem
aligner: star_rsem
Pass that file when you run the pipeline:
nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq -r 3.27.0 \
  -params-file params.yaml \
  -profile docker
A parameter file records the data and analysis route chosen for a run.

title: What If You want Customize an nf-core Pipeline?
text:
5. Change Resource Settings with custom.config
Suppose STAR alignment fails because it runs out of memory. To request more resources only for STAR_ALIGN, create custom.config:
process {
  withName: 'NFCORE_RNASEQ:RNASEQ:ALIGN_STAR:STAR_ALIGN' {
    cpus = 16
    memory = 80.GB
  }
}
Then run:
nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq -r 3.27.0 \
  -params-file params.yaml \
  -profile docker \
  -c custom.config
This file changes the CPU and memory requested for the task; the machine or cluster must have those resources available. The withName selector targets a specific process, leaving the other steps at their configured settings.
On an existing HPC cluster, check whether nf-core already provides a profile for it. At the time of writing, nf-core/configs lists 158 shared configurations, including UPPMAX. On a supported UPPMAX cluster, -profile uppmax loads its settings.

title: What If You want Customize an nf-core Pipeline?
text:
6. When Should You Edit .nf Files?
Maintain your own pipeline version only when you need to insert a new step into the workflow, replace a tool that the pipeline does not support, or change how data passes between steps. For example, if a new module must run after per-sample quantification and feed its output into subsequent steps, you are changing the workflow, not just selecting parameters. If the new analysis only uses the pipeline’s final output, run it separately after nf-core/rnaseq finishes.
The practical order is simple: check built-in parameters first, adjust runtime configuration if needed, and edit .nf files only when the workflow itself must change.

title: Nextflow: Local Server, Cluster, or Cloud computation?
text:
3 min read
Nextflow shines when it comes to resource management, natively supporting everything from your local machine and local HPC clusters to top-tier cloud platforms. You can easily tailor your compute environment to match your specific project scale.
For small-scale tasks, a local setup does the trick. Just install Nextflow on your machine, configure your environment variables, and you’re good to go.
For heavy workloads, scaling out to a compute cluster is the way to go. Nextflow seamlessly integrates with popular schedulers like Slurm, SGE, and LSF. All you need to do is specify the scheduler and its parameters in your configuration file. Tip: You can check out nf-core/configs, where the community has already shared production-ready setups for 158 institutional clusters.
If you want to tap into cloud computing for its limitless scalability and elastic provisioning, Nextflow has you covered. You can spin up VMs on AWS or GCP, install Nextflow, and configure your cloud credentials and resource types.
Here is a quick walkthrough of how it works on AWS:
Currently, Nextflow’s official community plugins only support native integration with AWS and GCP, which is a bit of a bummer for users based in China. On top of that, for biotech companies unfamiliar with cloud resource management, handling the initial setup and day-to-day DevOps for Nextflow can be a real headache.
But look at the bright side—the payoffs for enterprises are massive. It completely takes the burden off your IT operations team, keeping them out of the weeds of complex infrastructure management. More importantly, it dramatically shrinks the turnaround time from “raw sequencing data” to “actionable insights.” By offloading the heavy lifting of infrastructure, your core scientific teams can focus entirely on what they do best: biological innovation and breakthroughs, driving true cost-efficiency in a highly competitive market.

AWS cloud scaling: nextflow run main.nf -profile aws_cloud

title: The Stupidest Machine Learning Mistakes in Bioinformatics
text:
10 min read
Your model has an AUROC of 0.98. The heatmap looks beautiful. The top genes have plausible biological functions.
Then you try another cohort. The performance falls apart.
Before replacing logistic regression with a transformer, inspect the experiment around the model. A sophisticated algorithm can learn a very simple mistake.
This post takes inspiration from the practical mistake-and-correction format of Chatomics’ bioinformatics mistakes article. The examples below are original teaching scenarios, not claims about experiments I have performed. “Stupid” describes a preventable workflow mistake, not the person making it.

title: The Stupidest Machine Learning Mistakes in Bioinformatics
text:
1. Selecting genes before cross-validation
What you meant to do: Find a compact expression signature that predicts disease in new patients.
What you actually did: Use every patient’s disease label to select differentially expressed genes, then cross-validate a classifier on that fixed gene list.
The held-out patients have already helped choose the inputs. Cross-validation of the final classifier does not undo that information leak. This issue was documented in microarray classification more than two decades ago by Ambroise and McLachlan (2002).
Correction: Repeat supervised gene selection within each training fold. A gene list fixed independently of this dataset is a different situation; record where it came from.
# WRONG: validation labels influence the selected genes.
X_selected = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=100).fit_transform(X, y)
cross_val_score(classifier, X_selected, y, cv=cv, groups=patient_id)

# BETTER: the selector is fitted separately inside each fold.
model = make_pipeline(
    SelectKBest(f_classif, k=100),
    StandardScaler(),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000),
)
cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=cv, groups=patient_id)
These are workflow excerpts; imports and an explicit grouped splitter appear below. A pipeline protects the operations inside it. It cannot repair a leaked gene list prepared outside it.



Feature selection outside versus inside cross-validation


Figure 1. Original schematic. The top workflow lets validation labels influence gene selection. In the bottom workflow, each fold learns its own selector and scaler from training data only. No performance values are implied.

title: The Stupidest Machine Learning Mistakes in Bioinformatics
section: 2. Splitting rows when you should split patients
text:
2. Splitting rows when you should split patients
What you meant to do: Predict an outcome for a patient the model has never seen.
What you actually did: Randomly split cells, pathology tiles, or repeated visits. Different observations from the same patient appear on both sides.
The model may exploit patient-specific expression, staining, or acquisition characteristics. A row-level score now answers a different question: can it predict more observations from partly familiar patients?
Correction: Keep the relevant independent unit together. For new-patient prediction, group by patient; for new-center deployment, also test a held-out center. For protein prediction, consider whether homologous sequences crossing the split undermine the intended claim.
Scikit-learn’s cross-validation guide explains grouped and time-ordered splitting. Stratifying labels does not itself separate patients.



Row-level and patient-level split


Figure 2. Original schematic. Letters A–D represent patients. Keeping all observations from one patient in the same partition prevents direct patient overlap; it does not guarantee freedom from center or batch confounding.

title: The Stupidest Machine Learning Mistakes in Bioinformatics
section: 3. Learning preprocessing from the entire cohort
text:
3. Learning preprocessing from the entire cohort
What you meant to do: Make features comparable before training.
What you actually did: Fit imputation, scaling, PCA, or data-driven batch adjustment on the whole cohort, then evaluate held-out samples.
Even without disease labels, a fitted transformation can use information about the evaluation distribution. For ordinary prediction of unseen samples, training data should determine the transformation. The official pitfalls guide explicitly includes scaling, imputation, PCA, and feature selection in its leakage discussion.
Correction: Fit learned transformations inside training folds; apply the fitted transformation to validation samples. Distinguish this from sample-local transformations, such as a fixed log transform, that do not estimate parameters from other samples.
Jointly integrating training and test cohorts can be appropriate for an explicitly transductive task, but it does not establish performance on future samples unavailable during fitting. Ask how a genuinely new sample would pass through the saved workflow.

title: The Stupidest Machine Learning Mistakes in Bioinformatics
text:
4. Applying SMOTE before splitting
What you meant to do: Help the model learn a rare positive class.
What you actually did: Resample the complete dataset before cross-validation. Synthetic examples can depend on observations later assigned to validation, and evaluation no longer reflects the original class distribution.
Correction: Resample only the training portion of each fold. Keep validation and test observations untouched. An imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline handles samplers during fitting; the imbalanced-learn pitfalls guide demonstrates why resampling the whole dataset is problematic.
For a small, high-dimensional omics cohort, SMOTE is not automatically a good idea. A synthetic point between patients need not represent a biologically plausible patient. Compare against class weighting and a simple baseline before adopting it.

title: The Stupidest Machine Learning Mistakes in Bioinformatics
section: 5. Tuning until the test set agrees with you
text:
5. Tuning until the test set agrees with you
What you meant to do: Obtain an honest final performance estimate.
What you actually did: Try 30 gene panels, five algorithms, and several seeds; inspect the test score after each change; publish the winner.
The test set has become a model-selection tool. Cawley and Talbot (2010) explain how selection can overfit a noisy evaluation criterion, even when individual models are regularized.
Correction: Use development folds for tuning and keep a final test cohort untouched until the workflow is frozen. With limited samples, use nested cross-validation: the inner loop selects the model; the outer loop estimates the performance of that selection procedure. See the official nested-CV example.
Choosing the best random seed is also selection. Predeclare seeds or report the distribution across a planned set. The largest score is not a reproducibility strategy.

title: The Stupidest Machine Learning Mistakes in Bioinformatics
section: 6. Celebrating 99% accuracy while finding zero positives
text:
6. Celebrating 99% accuracy while finding zero positives
What you meant to do: Detect a rare outcome.
What you actually did: Report accuracy without examining the confusion matrix.
Consider 1,000 samples with 10 positives. A model that predicts “negative” for everyone has 99% accuracy and 0% recall. This is arithmetic, not a simulated benchmark.



Confusion matrices illustrating the accuracy trap


Figure 3. Constructed example, not patient data. Model A predicts everyone negative. Model B finds eight of ten positives but produces 40 false positives. B has lower accuracy; whether its trade-off is acceptable depends on the intended use.
Correction: State prevalence, show confusion counts, and report metrics suited to the task. Precision-recall summaries can be informative when positives are rare; their baseline and interpretation depend on prevalence. AUROC measures ranking, not performance at a chosen operating threshold. The metric guide defines these quantities.
Also compare with a DummyClassifier. Beating no baseline is an easy way to impress yourself.

title: The Stupidest Machine Learning Mistakes in Bioinformatics
text:
7. Treating 0.5 as a scientific threshold
What you meant to do: Turn a risk score into an actionable decision.
What you actually did: Accept the library’s default cutoff and interpret a score of 0.9 as a trustworthy 90% probability.
Ranking, calibration, and decision-making are separate properties. A model can rank samples well while producing poor probability estimates. Inspect a reliability diagram; the calibration guide explains this distinction. Brier score is useful, but it reflects more than calibration alone.
Correction: Select a threshold using a stated objective and development data, then evaluate that fixed threshold on held-out data. Do not optimize it on the final test set. The threshold guide shows why changing the cutoff changes decisions without changing the underlying probability scores.
Calibration also needs separation from model fitting and final evaluation. Recheck it when cohort composition or prevalence changes.

title: The Stupidest Machine Learning Mistakes in Bioinformatics
section: 8. Training a batch detector and calling it a disease model
text:
8. Training a batch detector and calling it a disease model
What you meant to do: Learn biology associated with disease.
What you actually did: Collect all cases in one laboratory and all controls in another, then randomly split the combined dataset.
Both partitions preserve the same technical shortcut. A high test score may reflect the laboratory, processing date, or assay rather than disease.
This is more than a hypothetical concern: Zech et al. (2018) found that pneumonia models could exploit hospital information and did not consistently generalize across sites. Applying that lesson to omics is an analogy, not a result reported in that imaging paper.
Correction: Audit outcome-by-batch tables, compare metadata-only baselines, and evaluate relevant external cohorts. If batch and disease are perfectly confounded, a batch-correction button cannot establish which signal was biological. You need a design that separates them.
Likewise, a prognosis model must use information available at the stated prediction time. Post-outcome measurements can make an impossible prediction look easy.

title: The Stupidest Machine Learning Mistakes in Bioinformatics
section: 9. Turning feature importance into a mechanism
text:
9. Turning feature importance into a mechanism
What you meant to do: Understand why the model predicts well.
What you actually did: Label the highest-ranked gene a disease driver.
Feature importance describes a model’s behavior under an explanation procedure. It does not by itself identify a causal biological mechanism. Coexpressed genes also complicate interpretation: if one gene substitutes for another, permuting either alone may have little effect.
Correction: Assess importance on held-out data, inspect correlated feature groups, and check stability across folds or cohorts. The permutation-importance guide and its correlated-feature example explain why a useful predictor can still receive low permutation importance.
Use an important gene as a candidate for follow-up, and state the additional evidence needed for a mechanistic claim.

title: The Stupidest Machine Learning Mistakes in Bioinformatics
section: 10. Losing sample identity in a perfectly valid array
text:
10. Losing sample identity in a perfectly valid array
What you meant to do: Match each expression profile to its label.
What you actually did: Sort the expression table, leave metadata in its original order, convert both to NumPy, and start training.
Everything has the right shape. Nothing has the right patient.
Correction: Join by explicit identifiers, reject duplicates, and assert order before dropping labels. Keep feature names and their order with the fitted model too.
# X_df: samples × genes; metadata: one row per sample_id.
assert X_df.index.is_unique
assert metadata["sample_id"].is_unique
meta = metadata.set_index("sample_id").loc[X_df.index]
assert X_df.index.equals(meta.index)
assert meta["outcome"].notna().all()
y = meta["outcome"].to_numpy()
For longitudinal data, use a unique observation ID for alignment and a separate patient ID for splitting. Do not force multiple visits into a one-row-per-patient assumption.

title: The Stupidest Machine Learning Mistakes in Bioinformatics
text:
A small workflow worth keeping
The following is a template for binary classification with patient groups, not a complete omics pipeline or a benchmark. X must already be correctly aligned, numeric, and free of missing values; y is binary and patient_id identifies groups. Ensure sufficient class representation and groups in every fold. Set k to suit the available features.
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedGroupKFold, cross_validate
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

cv = StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
for train, valid in cv.split(X, y, groups=patient_id):
    assert not (set(patient_id[train]) & set(patient_id[valid]))
    assert len(np.unique(y[train])) == len(np.unique(y[valid])) == 2

model = make_pipeline(
    SelectKBest(f_classif, k=100),
    StandardScaler(),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000),
)
scores = cross_validate(
    model, X, y, groups=patient_id, cv=cv,
    scoring={"auroc": "roc_auc", "ap": "average_precision"},
)
print(scores["test_auroc"])
print(scores["test_ap"])
This evaluates a fixed workflow. If you use these scores to choose k, regularization, or algorithms, add an inner selection loop and retain an outer evaluation loop. Five correlated fold scores are not five independent experiments or automatically a confidence interval. These snippets were checked for syntax, not run against a biological dataset.

title: The Stupidest Machine Learning Mistakes in Bioinformatics
section: Before believing the next impressive score
text:
Before believing the next impressive score
Ask four questions: Who is held out? What information crossed the boundary? Which decision does the metric support? Can a simpler explanation account for the result?
Save the split IDs, feature schema, preprocessing objects, environment versions, and selection history. A fixed seed helps replay a workflow; it does not make the workflow valid.
The most expensive mistake is often the one that produces a beautiful figure and no error message.

title: The Stupidest Mistakes in Machine Learning
text:
13 min read
The program runs. The loss decreases. A checkpoint lands in your output directory.
None of these tells you whether the experiment makes sense.
Some machine learning mistakes produce an exception. The expensive ones produce a convincing chart. You can spend a week tuning a model that is solving the wrong problem, then spend another week explaining its success.
This is a practical collection of ten mistakes, informed by researchers’ experience essays, original papers, and framework documentation. The scenarios and illustrations are original; they are not experiments reported by those authors. “Stupid” describes an avoidable mistake, not the person making it.

title: The Stupidest Mistakes in Machine Learning
section: 1. Choosing a model before understanding the data
text:
1. Choosing a model before understanding the data
What you meant to do: Solve a prediction problem.
What you actually did: Choose a fashionable architecture before inspecting how examples and labels were produced.
A folder named clean_data is not evidence of clean data. A missing value encoded as -999 can become a strong feature. Two annotators may use different definitions of “positive.” A timestamp may record upload time rather than the event you want to forecast.
Sambasivan and colleagues’ Data Cascades study documents how neglected data work causes compounding downstream problems. Its findings come from interviews with practitioners, not a universal statistical law.
Correction: Inspect examples from each label, source, and time period. Read the labeling instructions. Plot missingness and investigate duplicates. Write down what one row represents and what the target actually measures.
When you see -999, establish whether it is a missing-value sentinel or a valid measurement before deciding how to handle it. Feeding an unchecked sentinel to a transformer can make the model learn an encoding convention you never intended it to use.

Correct data must also be available at prediction time
Ask a second question of the same data: Was this feature actually available at prediction time? Random splits of dependent observations and features built from later records can make evaluation misrepresent the intended forecasting task.
A “number of purchases in the next seven days” column might have an innocent name in a feature table. It is still unavailable at today’s prediction time. An event timestamp does not necessarily equal the time the system learned about that event.
Correction: Write down when the prediction is made and what data is available then. Build features using only records already available at that moment, and evaluate on later observations. If outcome windows overlap, check what the partitions share. Splitting by time cannot remove future information already baked into a feature.
Martin Zinkevich’s Rules of Machine Learning recommends testing on data collected after the training period. The exact split should reflect your application and dependence structure.

title: The Stupidest Mistakes in Machine Learning
section: 2. Beating a baseline you never allowed to compete
text:
2. Beating a baseline you never allowed to compete
What you meant to do: Show that a new model improves prediction.
What you actually did: Tune your proposed method extensively, compare it against a poorly configured baseline, and call the difference an architectural advance.
In their 2019 analysis of neural recommendation approaches, Ferrari Dacrema, Cremonesi, and Jannach showed that adequately tuned simpler approaches could outperform several reproduced neural methods. That is evidence about the methods and benchmarks studied, not proof that neural networks never help.
Correction: Give baselines a defensible tuning budget, the same information, and the same evaluation protocol. Include a task-specific heuristic: predicting the last observed value for forecasting, for example. Report compute and latency alongside predictive quality.
“Default settings” is not a fair handicap to impose only on the competitor.

title: The Stupidest Mistakes in Machine Learning
section: 3. Scaling up before fitting a tiny training batch
text:
3. Scaling up before fitting a tiny training batch
What you meant to do: Train a useful neural network.
What you actually did: Launch a large run before checking whether a few examples can be learned at all.
Karpathy’s training recipe recommends inspecting the actual tensors and deliberately overfitting a small batch as a debugging step.
Correction: Remove augmentation, simplify the model, and train on a fixed handful of unambiguous examples. With enough capacity and compatible labels, fitting them should be possible. Failure is a reason to investigate labels, loss, gradients, and optimization—not a proof that your model needs another GPU.
If the tiny batch will not fit, print the original records, transformed features, and labels. Check for identical inputs with conflicting targets. For a deterministic binary predictor given the same input once with each label, ordinary unweighted binary cross-entropy is minimized at a shared probability of 0.5, with mean loss log(2) rather than zero. This calculation does not cover every multilabel or context-dependent setup.
Also inspect regularization, capacity, learning rate, and gradients. Failure to fit does not diagnose duplicate-label errors by itself. Successful memorization remains a debugging check, not evidence of generalization.

title: The Stupidest Mistakes in Machine Learning
text:
4. Letting broadcasting rewrite your objective
What you meant to do: Compare each prediction with its corresponding target.
What you actually did: Subtract a prediction array shaped (N, 1) from targets shaped (N,).
Under PyTorch’s broadcasting rules, this subtraction produces an (N, N) matrix. You are comparing every prediction with every target.
# Both arrays describe one scalar per example, but shapes differ.
pred = torch.tensor([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0]])  # (3, 1)
target = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])      # (3,)
wrong = ((pred - target) ** 2).mean()      # 4/3, not zero

assert pred.ndim == 2 and pred.shape[1] == 1
assert target.ndim == 1 and pred.shape[0] == target.shape[0]
pred = pred.squeeze(-1)
assert pred.shape == target.shape
right = ((pred - target) ** 2).mean()      # zero
This is a PyTorch illustration; the companion standard-library script reproduces the arithmetic without PyTorch. It does not train a neural network.



Correct paired errors and unintended pairwise errors


Figure 1. Calculated teaching example. Matching predictions [1, 2, 3] give zero paired error, but the broadcasted objective includes all nine pairwise errors and has mean 4/3.
Correction: Check that each example has exactly one output before adjusting the shape. Even for a single example, (1, 1).squeeze(-1) becomes (1,), preserving the batch axis. Unconditional flatten() can hide a multi-output mistake by flattening everything. If other code needs the two-dimensional predictions, keep the adjusted result in a separate variable.
The wrong loss can still decrease. For independently adjustable predictions, the all-pairs objective pulls every prediction toward the target mean. Convergence does not establish that the objective was right.

title: The Stupidest Mistakes in Machine Learning
text:
5. Applying softmax because “classification needs probabilities”
What you meant to do: Train a multiclass classifier.
What you actually did: Apply softmax, then pass the resulting probabilities to CrossEntropyLoss.
Distinguish the two arguments in CrossEntropyLoss(input, target). The PyTorch documentation specifies:







Argument
Expected representation




input: model predictions
Raw logits; do not apply softmax first


target: supervision
Integer class indices, or valid same-shaped class probabilities (soft labels)



Soft-label support concerns target; it does not change the prediction-side contract. Passing softmax(logits) as input makes the loss treat those numbers as logits and apply log-softmax to them again. The code can run while computing a different objective.
# Classification with one integer class label per example.
logits = model(x)                       # (batch, classes)
loss = criterion(logits, y)             # criterion = CrossEntropyLoss()
probabilities = logits.softmax(dim=-1)  # for inspecting predictions
Correction: Check shapes, dtypes, and values separately for predictions and targets. Class-index targets ordinarily use long; soft targets use floating point and should be nonnegative distributions summing to one across classes. The documentation warns that the framework does not fully validate probability targets. Apply softmax for inspecting predictions outside the loss calculation.
For uniform predictions over C classes, ordinary unweighted cross-entropy is log(C): about 0.693 for two classes and 2.303 for ten. The result also holds for valid soft targets, including uniform targets: their probabilities sum to one, so -sum(q * log(1/C)) = log(C). This assumes no class weighting and a mean of the per-example losses.

title: The Stupidest Mistakes in Machine Learning
section: 6. Confusing evaluation mode with disabled gradients
text:
6. Confusing evaluation mode with disabled gradients
What you meant to do: Measure a trained model’s validation performance.
What you actually did: Wrap prediction in no_grad() and assume that also switches dropout and batch normalization into evaluation behavior.
These controls do different jobs. model.eval() changes the behavior of relevant modules. Autograd modes control gradient recording; they do not automatically select evaluation mode.
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    logits = model(x_valid)
    validation_loss = criterion(logits, y_valid)
model.train()  # restore training behavior before the next training phase
Correction: Set both intentionally. With standard running-statistics batch normalization, validation in training mode can update those statistics. Some applications deliberately use stochastic inference; that needs an explicit protocol rather than an accidental mode setting.

title: The Stupidest Mistakes in Machine Learning
section: 7. Reporting the luckiest seed as the algorithm
text:
7. Reporting the luckiest seed as the algorithm
What you meant to do: Compare two learning methods.
What you actually did: Run each several times, select its best score, and omit the rest.
Bouthillier and colleagues examine multiple sources of variation in benchmark results. Agarwal and colleagues show why uncertainty matters particularly when deep reinforcement learning is evaluated with few runs. Their specific recommendations concern their experimental settings; they should not become a mechanical “five seeds is enough” rule.
Correction: Plan repetitions, preserve all runs, and distinguish initialization variability from sampling, splitting, and tuning variability. Use paired comparisons where the design supports them. Choose uncertainty estimates that match the unit of replication.
A fixed seed aids debugging. It cannot guarantee identical outcomes across environments: the PyTorch reproducibility notes explain the limitations.

title: The Stupidest Mistakes in Machine Learning
section: 8. Letting the average hide the failure
text:
8. Letting the average hide the failure
What you meant to do: Improve the model for its intended users.
What you actually did: Celebrate one aggregate score without checking meaningful subgroups or conditions.
Here is a constructed example with 900 easy cases and 100 difficult cases:



Evaluation slice
Model A correct
Model B correct




Easy cases, n = 900
855 (95%)
882 (98%)


Difficult cases, n = 100
80 (80%)
60 (60%)


All cases, n = 1,000
935 (93.5%)
942 (94.2%)



The aggregate improves by 0.7 percentage points while the difficult slice loses 20 points. This is subgroup performance degradation: an update reduces performance for a particular subgroup while the aggregate improves. Because easy cases account for 90% of observations, their gain outweighs the difficult group’s loss.
This describes the observed behavior. The table alone cannot identify whether training representation, optimization preferences, or another factor caused the decline, and does not diagnose majority bias. The aggregate improvement is real, but the benefit is not shared by every group.



Aggregate improvement and deterioration on a smaller evaluation slice


Figure 2. Constructed counts, not measured model performance. The shared vertical scale makes the subgroup decline visible.
Correction: Predefine important slices, report their sizes and uncertainty, and inspect error cases. Avoid selecting only favorable slices after seeing results. A small subgroup estimate may be unstable.
D’Amour and colleagues’ underspecification paper supplies a related warning: similarly strong in-domain scores can coexist with different deployment behavior. One number cannot specify everything you need from a model.

title: The Stupidest Mistakes in Machine Learning
text:
9. Treating preprocessing as an afterthought
What you meant to do: Prepare the inputs, then measure performance on unseen examples.
What you actually did: Fit a global StandardScaler or target encoder before splitting training and validation data. Alternatively, create augmented copies first, then randomly split those copies.
The symptom: Training runs smoothly and validation performance looks unusually good—perhaps even 99% accuracy. That number is a warning to investigate, not a diagnostic test for leakage.
A globally fitted scaler uses validation feature means and variances. Target encoding can additionally use validation labels to define category values. Augmented versions of the same original can cross the split and make the validation examples partly familiar. These are different leakage routes, with different consequences. See the official preprocessing pitfalls guide.
Correction: Split independent originals first. Fit learned preprocessing on training data, then apply it unchanged to validation data. Within cross-validation, repeat fitting inside every training fold. Keep related augmented copies in their original’s partition; training augmentation must preserve the task’s label semantics.
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# WRONG: validation observations influence the scaler.
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
X_train, X_valid, y_train, y_valid = train_test_split(
    X_scaled, y, stratify=y, random_state=42,
)

# RIGHT for independent observations: split before fitting.
X_train, X_valid, y_train, y_valid = train_test_split(
    X, y, stratify=y, random_state=42,
)
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_valid_scaled = scaler.transform(X_valid)
These are illustrative excerpts, not executed model results. Replace the random split when groups or time require another protocol. In cross-validation, put the scaler inside the pipeline rather than fitting it once before the folds.



Preprocessing and augmentation must respect the split


Figure 3. Original schematic. Training learns the transformation; validation only receives it. Augmented siblings stay with their original. No accuracy values are measured here.
Target encoding must not use a row’s own answer to encode that row. Even within the training set, a row’s own label can leak into its category statistic. Scikit-learn’s TargetEncoder uses internal cross-fitting in fit_transform; this is intentionally different from fit(...).transform(...). Its worked example illustrates why that distinction matters.
from sklearn.preprocessing import TargetEncoder

# X_cat_train / X_cat_valid contain categorical features only.
encoder = TargetEncoder(target_type="binary", random_state=42)
# Training: cross-fit internally so a row does not encode its own label.
X_cat_train_encoded = encoder.fit_transform(X_cat_train, y_train)
# Independent validation: apply the mapping learned from all training data;
# validation labels are never used.
X_cat_valid_encoded = encoder.transform(X_cat_valid)
You still need independent validation even if the encoder uses internal cross-fitting. If people have repeated records or observations follow a time order, the internal splits must respect those constraints too.
Leakage does not always produce 99% accuracy; its effect depends on the data and model. If a score looks suspicious, check the order of operations and rerun the evaluation with a clean workflow.

Use the same processing when the model goes live
Avoiding leakage during training is only part of the job. Saving weights while forgetting the scaler, feature order, vocabulary, or missing-value rules can still break predictions in production.
A feature called duration might mean seconds offline and milliseconds online. Both are numbers, so the program may not complain.
Save preprocessing and feature definitions with the model. Use a few fixed inputs to compare offline and online predictions. Sculley and colleagues’ technical-debt paper discusses these maintenance problems around the model.

title: The Stupidest Mistakes in Machine Learning
section: 10. Assuming the model merely observes the world
text:
10. Assuming the model merely observes the world
What you meant to do: Learn from historical behavior and improve future decisions.
What you actually did: Ignore that deploying the prediction system changes the data it later observes.
A recommender shows an item; exposure makes a click possible; the next training set records those clicks. An unseen item receives no click, but that does not tell you whether a user would have liked it. Repeatedly retraining can reinforce the old exposure policy.



Prediction, action, and newly observed data form a feedback loop


Figure 4. Original conceptual diagram. The logged observations depend on both user response and what the system chose to expose.
Perdomo and colleagues’ Performative Prediction studies how predictions change subsequent data. It offers a way to analyze that problem, rather than a ready-made fix for every exposure issue in recommendation.
Correction: Log what was shown and how it was selected, not just what was clicked. Where appropriate, use a controlled experiment to test whether a different recommendation policy helps. Clicks collected under the old policy may not tell you how the new one would perform.

title: The Stupidest Mistakes in Machine Learning
section: Three checks you can run without a GPU
text:
Three checks you can run without a GPU
The companion verification script checks the broadcasted squared-error arithmetic, the uniform-prediction cross-entropy reference, and the subgroup table. It uses only Python’s standard library. Run it from this article’s directory:
python3 examples/verify_examples.py
Those checks verify the constructed examples. They do not validate a model, and the PyTorch snippets above are illustrative excerpts rather than a complete training program.
A practical debugging order is: inspect actual inputs and labels, establish a fair baseline, check the objective and modes, test a tiny training case, then evaluate the full workflow under realistic conditions. Record the intended question alongside every reported score.
The mistake to fear is the one that produces exactly the result you hoped for, before you have checked why.
