title: scRNA-seq: Tracing the Barcode Disagreement Between Cell Ranger and Simpleaf
text:
Why this question
Nextflow orchestrates and records each analysis, and nf-core/scrnaseq offers several standardized routes for processing single-cell RNA-seq data. I wanted to know: given the same sequencing data, why do different routes retain slightly different sets of cells? Are the extra barcodes real cells, ambient RNA, or low-quality droplets? And do they change any biological conclusion?

title: scRNA-seq: Tracing the Barcode Disagreement Between Cell Ranger and Simpleaf
text:
Methods
The data are the public 10x PBMC 1k v3 dataset, processed with nf-core/scrnaseq 4.2.0. Both routes used the same FASTQ files and the GRCh38-2024-A reference: Cell Ranger used the prebuilt index, and Simpleaf built its own index from the FASTA/GTF in the same package.
Versions: Cell Ranger 10.0.0, Simpleaf 0.19.5, QCatch 0.2.12. The comparison is Cell Ranger versus Simpleaf + QCatch: Simpleaf produces the counts, and QCatch performs the subsequent cell calling.
Upstream processing ran on an AWS r6i.4xlarge instance (16 vCPU, 128 GiB). A CloudFormation template installed the software, ran the analysis, uploaded the results, and then terminated the instance automatically. The successful run took 84 minutes end to end. The bill came to about $2.05 including three failed attempts; the successful run alone cost about $1.41. All downstream comparisons for this sample ran on a personal Mac with 8 GB of RAM.

title: scRNA-seq: Tracing the Barcode Disagreement Between Cell Ranger and Simpleaf
text:
1. Which barcodes differ?
I first compared three barcode sets: retained by both, by Cell Ranger only, and by Simpleaf + QCatch only.
# Read both filtered results and harmonize the barcode suffix
shared = cr_cells & sa_cells
cr_only = cr_cells - sa_cells
sa_only = sa_cells - cr_cells

print(len(shared), len(cr_only), len(sa_only))
# 1221 0 7
print(len(shared) / len(cr_cells | sa_cells))
# 0.9943: intersection / union
All 7 barcodes sit in the transition zone between cells and background.



Barcode-rank plots with a zoom on the knee: green markers are the 7 barcodes retained only by Simpleaf + QCatch


The x-axis is barcode rank by UMI count; the y-axis is UMI count. In the right panel, open circles are Cell Ranger and diamonds are Simpleaf; a line joins the two values for the same barcode. The 500-UMI line is the testing threshold of this implementation, not a fixed value for every EmptyDrops analysis.
Measured as intersection over union, the two cell sets agree at 99.4%. Among shared cells, the Spearman correlation of total UMIs per cell is 0.9997, and Simpleaf counts are about 5% higher on average. Overall agreement is very high, but small differences can decide whether a borderline barcode is kept.
Note also that the two “raw matrices” in the figure contain 329,735 and 72,612 barcodes. They were retained under different upstream rules, so they cannot be treated as the same universe of droplets.

title: scRNA-seq: Tracing the Barcode Disagreement Between Cell Ranger and Simpleaf
section: 3. Different cell-calling algorithms, or different input counts?
text:
3. Different cell-calling algorithms, or different input counts?
I re-called cells in both matrices with the same QCatch code and parameters, using the OrdMag + EmptyDrops framework.
# Excerpt of QCatch internals; m is a CountMatrix, cc is the cell-calling module.
# Imports, versions and matrix conversion are in analysis/; this is not a standalone script.
initial = cc.initial_filtering_OrdMag(m, "10X_3p_v3", None)
res = cc.find_nonambient_barcodes(m, initial, "10X_3p_v3", None)
called = {b.decode() for b in initial} | set(res.eval_bcs[res.is_nonambient])
The Cell Ranger matrix still yields 1,221 cells and the Simpleaf matrix still yields 1,228, each identical barcode for barcode to the original results. Changing the random seed and the number of simulations did not remove the disagreement either.
The same implementation still disagrees, so the next place to look is the input matrices. The input differences, however, include both the counts and the range of background barcodes, so the disagreement cannot be attributed to a single factor.

Three barcodes crossed the 500-UMI threshold
Barcodes 1, 5 and 6 have fewer than 500 UMIs in the Cell Ranger matrix, so they never enter this step’s test against the ambient background; in the Simpleaf matrix they exceed the threshold. DHFR accounts for a substantial share of the extra counts.

The DHFR difference also appears in the shared cells: Simpleaf counts 45,624 UMIs (45,532 of them unspliced), whereas Cell Ranger counts 739. I then examined the DHFR region in the Cell Ranger BAM:
from collections import Counter
import pysam

# BAM_URL and BAI_URL are temporary access links to an existing BAM and its index.
with pysam.AlignmentFile(BAM_URL, index_filename=BAI_URL) as bam:
    mapq = Counter(r.mapping_quality
                   for r in bam.fetch("chr5", 80626226, 80655002))
print(mapq)
# Counter({1: 4718, 3: 2747, 255: 1519, 0: 4})
About 83% of the alignment records have MAPQ below 255. These records are concentrated in a single ~200 bp intronic window, with NH tags of 2–4: each read aligns to 2–4 locations in the genome.
A repeated sequence is the lead for the anomalous DHFR counts. The two routes use different reference targets and different alignment/assignment rules, which may send these reads to different places. I did not verify Simpleaf’s read-by-read assignment, so the mechanism remains an inference, and the chr8 lncRNA cannot be assumed to share the same cause by analogy.
Note: Cell Ranger adjusts MAPQ according to gene assignment, so its behavior cannot be reduced to “counting only uniquely mapped genomic alignments”. MAPQ = 255 does not necessarily mean the original STAR alignment had a single location. See the 10x BAM tag documentation.


The other four sit near the statistical threshold
Barcodes 2, 3 and 4 are all tested, but their adjusted p-values go from about 0.004 with Cell Ranger to about 0.0001 with Simpleaf, crossing this run’s 0.001 threshold. Barcode 7 is also near the threshold. I found no single clear source for these; for now the explanation stops at the statistical threshold rather than at the level of individual reads.

title: scRNA-seq: Tracing the Barcode Disagreement Between Cell Ranger and Simpleaf
text:
Finally: do these 7 barcodes matter?
For cell-type proportions: almost not at all. I held the counts, clustering and annotation fixed and changed only the cell set. The 7 extra barcodes fall into 4 groups: 2 platelets, 2 cDCs, 1 FCGR3A monocyte and 2 low-quality barcodes. Every other cell type keeps exactly the same number of cells; only the denominator grows from 1,221 to 1,228, diluting their proportions by at most 0.16 percentage points. After a common QC filter (≥ 200 genes, ≤ 20% mitochondrial), only 3 cells differ: 2 cDCs and 1 FCGR3A monocyte.
How small is that change? As controls, I changed only the clustering random seed, or only the count matrix, within the same workflow:



Largest change in each cell type’s proportion when only one factor changes


Blue: only the cell set changes; orange: only the clustering random seed (0–4); green: only the count matrix (Cell Ranger or Simpleaf).
The cell set shifts proportions by at most 0.16 percentage points, whereas the random seed or the count matrix shifts the monocyte and NK/CD8 T proportions by 6–10 percentage points. The latter two reflect my simple clustering/annotation approach and should not be generalized into a difference between the tools. The sensitivity of the annotation to analysis settings deserves more scrutiny than these 7 barcodes.
For markers of small cell populations: some effect, but limited. The cDC population has only 16 cells, so 2 more is a 12.5% increase.



Expression fraction and adjusted p-value of cDC markers


The conclusions for CST3, FCER1A and CLEC10A are unchanged. CD1C weakens: its expression fraction drops from 63% to 56% and its adjusted p-value rises from 0.012 to 0.034, because the 2 added cells do not express CD1C. In addition, after QC both sides contain the same 15 platelets, yet PPBP’s marker rank moves from 13th to 1st because the top genes have nearly tied scores. When reading markers, look at expression fraction, effect size and statistical evidence, not rank alone.

title: scRNA-seq: Tracing the Barcode Disagreement Between Cell Ranger and Simpleaf
text:
Conclusion
From the same FASTQ files, Cell Ranger retains 1,221 cells and Simpleaf + QCatch retains 1,228, with the former entirely contained in the latter. I traced the 7 extra barcodes: 3 crossed the UMI threshold because of extra counts, with a repeated sequence in a DHFR intron as an important lead; the other 4 sit near the statistical threshold. Changing only the cell set shifts cell-type proportions by at most 0.16 percentage points. These 7 barcodes have little effect on overall cell-type proportions, but a few genes combined with fixed thresholds are enough to decide whether a barcode is kept. Both comparisons used a single PBMC sample; whether the two workflows agree this closely on other data remains to be tested.

title: nf-core/sarek: From DNA Reads to Variant Discovery
section: A Swedish Name, a Practical Purpose
text:
A Swedish Name, a Practical Purpose
Sarek shares its name with a national park in northern Sweden. Early releases used names such as Ruotes and Skårki, giving the project a distinctive geographic identity. The connection appears in the developer’s 2020 presentation.
The workflow originated at SciLifeLab’s National Genomics Infrastructure (NGI) and National Bioinformatics Infrastructure Sweden (NBIS), with support from the Swedish Childhood Tumor Biobank. Developers at Germany’s QBiC later joined the project and contributed to its development and Nextflow DSL2 implementation.[1]
nf-core/sarek is a reproducible workflow for DNA variant discovery. It supports whole-genome, exome and targeted sequencing, with separate germline and somatic analysis routes. Depending on the selected tools, it detects small variants, structural variants, copy-number changes and microsatellite instability.
DNA sequencing produces reads that must be aligned to a reference genome before differences can be identified. Running this analysis manually requires coordinating software versions, file formats and computing environments. Sarek organizes these tasks into a consistent workflow:
Preprocessing → Variant calling → Annotation → Quality reporting.[1]

title: nf-core/sarek: From DNA Reads to Variant Discovery
text:
1. How Popular Is Sarek?
As checked on October 8, 2026, Sarek had approximately 612 GitHub stars, compared with roughly 1,400 for nf-core/rnaseq. These figures indicate community interest, rather than execution counts or analytical accuracy.[3]

title: nf-core/sarek: From DNA Reads to Variant Discovery
text:
2. Why Variant Analysis Matters
If the genome is an instruction manual, RNA expression analysis measures which sections are being read and how frequently. DNA variant analysis identifies changes to the text itself.
Its applications include:

Genetic disease research: identifying variants that may disrupt gene function.
Cancer research: detecting acquired mutations, amplifications and deletions.
Population genetics: studying genetic differences between individuals and their associations with traits.

A difference from the reference genome is not necessarily harmful. Many variants represent ordinary genetic variation; annotation, filtering and additional evidence are needed to assess their significance.

Sequencing approach

Sarek can start from raw reads, or from existing alignment or variant files at the appropriate entry point. It supports normal, tumor and additional relapse samples from the same patient. Initially developed for human and mouse data, it can also analyze other species with a suitable reference genome, compatible tools and annotation resources.[1]

4. Beyond Single-Base Changes








Analysis

Tool selection depends on the sample design, sequencing approach and biological question. These are optional analysis routes, rather than a list of tools that must all run together.[1]

title: nf-core/sarek: From DNA Reads to Variant Discovery
section: 5. Why Separate Germline and Somatic Routes?
text:
5. Why Separate Germline and Somatic Routes?
Germline analysis identifies constitutional variants, usually present in nearly all cells. These may be inherited or arise de novo.
Somatic analysis identifies variants acquired in a subset of cells. In cancer studies, comparing a tumor with a matched normal sample helps distinguish acquired changes from the individual’s germline background.
The statistical assumptions differ. At a diploid autosomal locus without copy-number changes, a heterozygous germline variant typically has a variant allele fraction (VAF) near 50%. Tumor samples contain mixtures of normal cells, cancer cells and tumor subclones, so genuine somatic variants may have much lower VAFs.
For example, if 20% of cells carry a heterozygous mutation and all cells are diploid at that locus, the expected VAF is:
\[
\mathrm{VAF} \approx 20\% \times \frac{1}{2} = 10\%
\]
The caller must distinguish this signal from sequencing or alignment errors. Germline and somatic detection therefore require different models and filters: HaplotypeCaller primarily targets germline variants, while Mutect2 targets somatic variants.[1]

title: nf-core/sarek: From DNA Reads to Variant Discovery
text:
6. Workflow
Figure 1 shows the germline and somatic routes, their shared processing stages and representative tools.



Sarek workflow showing germline and somatic preprocessing, variant calling, annotation and reporting


Figure 1. Sarek workflow overview (Sarek 3.5.1). Source: nf-core/sarek.[1]

Step 1: Preprocessing
Check read quality, optionally trim adapters, align reads to the reference genome, mark duplicates and perform base quality score recalibration where appropriate.[1]
These steps reduce misleading evidence: PCR copies are not independent observations, and incorrectly aligned reads can create apparent variants.


Step 2: Variant Calling
Select callers for the study design and variant classes of interest. Examples include HaplotypeCaller or DeepVariant for germline small variants, Mutect2 for somatic small variants, and Manta for structural variants.[1]


Step 3: Annotation
VEP and SnpEff add biological context, including affected genes and transcripts, amino-acid changes and predicted splice effects. Annotation translates genomic coordinates into potential functional consequences.[1]


Step 4: Reporting
Outputs include processed alignments, VCF files and tool-specific results. CNV and MSI analyses also generate their own tables or plots. MultiQC summarizes metrics such as coverage, alignment statistics and duplication rates.[1]






Tip



Execution report: records how the entire Nextflow pipeline ran, showing whether each step succeeded, along with its runtime and resource usage.

title: nf-core/sarek: From DNA Reads to Variant Discovery
text:
7. Reproducibility Across Computing Environments
Sarek uses Nextflow to coordinate tasks and containers to manage software environments. This supports consistent execution on local machines, clusters and cloud infrastructure, reducing the manual work required to connect individual tools.[1]

title: nf-core/atacseq: Mapping Accessible Chromatin with “Molecular Scissors”
text:
6 min read
Most nucleated cells in the human body share essentially the same DNA, yet perform different functions. Think of the genome as an instruction manual: different cells make different pages available to read.
ATAC-seq measures this accessibility. nf-core/atacseq turns the resulting sequencing data into outputs for quality assessment, sample comparison, and downstream analysis.

title: nf-core/atacseq: Mapping Accessible Chromatin with “Molecular Scissors”
section: 1. 2013: Turning a Library Preparation Tool into a Chromatin Probe
text:
1. 2013: Turning a Library Preparation Tool into a Chromatin Probe
ATAC-seq was not the first method for studying accessible chromatin. DNase-seq and other approaches were already in use when Buenrostro and colleagues introduced ATAC-seq in Nature Methods in 2013, offering a simpler experimental approach.[2]
Its key component is Tn5 transposase, which cuts DNA and inserts sequencing adapters. DNA packaging affects how easily Tn5 can reach it, so accessible regions are more readily tagged. Mapping the sequenced fragments back to the genome reveals where these regions are.[2] Experimental conditions and Tn5 sequence preferences also affect the signal, making quality control and statistical analysis essential.
Whereas ChIP-seq uses antibodies to map DNA associated with a specific protein or histone modification, ATAC-seq and DNase-seq profile chromatin accessibility without target-specific antibodies. By combining DNA fragmentation and adapter insertion, ATAC-seq generally requires fewer cells and fewer library preparation steps than conventional DNase-seq, making it useful when material is limited.

title: nf-core/atacseq: Mapping Accessible Chromatin with “Molecular Scissors”
section: 2. Fragment Lengths Tell a Story Too
text:
2. Fragment Lengths Tell a Story Too
ATAC-seq provides information beyond where fragments map. DNA wraps around histones to form nucleosomes, and fragment lengths can reflect this organization. Short fragments are often associated with nucleosome-free regions, while longer fragments can reflect DNA spanning one or more nucleosomes.[2]
The fragment length distribution therefore connects sequencing data to chromatin structure. In 2017, Corces and colleagues introduced Omni-ATAC, improving the signal-to-background ratio and extending the method to samples such as frozen tissues.[3] These developments have made chromatin accessibility profiling practical for a wider range of samples.

title: nf-core/atacseq: Mapping Accessible Chromatin with “Molecular Scissors”
section: 3. An Unexpected Connection to Cattle Research
text:
3. An Unexpected Connection to Cattle Research
The official credits identify Harshil Patel as the original developer. Björn Langer and Jose Espinosa-Carrasco later converted the pipeline to Nextflow DSL2 under the BovReg project.[1]
BovReg studies functional regulation in the cattle genome, examining how genetic and epigenetic variation relates to traits across breeds.[4]
Why study chromatin accessibility in cattle? DNA sequence alone cannot fully explain a trait. Understanding gene regulation also requires knowing which genomic regions are accessible in particular cells or conditions. ATAC-seq provides part of that information.

title: nf-core/atacseq: Mapping Accessible Chromatin with “Molecular Scissors”
section: 4. Workflow: From FASTQ to Chromatin Accessibility Profiles
text:
4. Workflow: From FASTQ to Chromatin Accessibility Profiles
This article covers version 2.1.2. In the official workflow diagram below, green represents analysis after merging libraries within each biological replicate; blue represents optional analysis after merging biological replicates within each condition. Square nodes indicate required steps, and circular nodes indicate optional steps.[1]



nf-core/atacseq 2.1.2 workflow diagram


Figure 1. nf-core/atacseq workflow overview (version 2.1.2). Source: nf-core/atacseq.[1]

4.1 Read Processing and Alignment
FastQC assesses the raw FASTQ files. Trim Galore! uses Cutadapt to remove adapters and trim low-quality bases, followed by another quality check. Alignment options include BWA (default), Bowtie2, STAR, and Chromap. In version 2.1.2, paired-end data aligned with Chromap do not proceed beyond alignment.[1,5]
Picard marks duplicates and merges sequencing runs belonging to the same biological replicate. Duplicates are marked again before filtering. SAMtools, BEDTools, BAMTools, and Pysam remove mitochondrial reads, reads overlapping blacklisted regions, duplicates, and unreliable alignments, and check paired-end read consistency. These steps reduce technical noise before peak calling.[1]


4.2 Analysis After Filtering








Task
Main tools
Purpose




Alignment and library QC
Picard, Preseq
Assess alignment quality and library complexity; estimate the benefit of deeper sequencing


Signal tracks
BEDTools, bedGraphToBigWig
Generate bigWig tracks scaled to one million mapped reads


Signal enrichment
deepTools
Examine signal around transcription start sites, across gene bodies, and genome-wide


Peak calling and annotation
MACS2, HOMER
Identify enriched regions and annotate their genomic context and nearby genes


Consensus regions and counting
BEDTools, featureCounts
Combine peaks into shared regions and count reads in each sample


Sample comparison and reporting
R/DESeq2, ataqv, MultiQC, IGV
Normalize counts, generate PCA and clustering plots, summarize QC, and visualize tracks



These tasks correspond to the alignment QC, enrichment, peak calling, and reporting branches in the official diagram.[1,5]


4.3 Three Details to Keep in Mind
Library merging and biological replicate merging serve different purposes. Repeated sequencing runs of the same biological replicate use identical sample and replicate values in the samplesheet and are merged after alignment. Biological replicates within a condition share the same sample value but have different replicate values. The blue branch pools these replicates to increase coverage for peak calling. Read counting against the resulting consensus peaks still uses the separate replicate alignments, preserving differences between replicates.[5] See the samplesheet documentation for details.
Peak calling and consensus filtering have specific defaults. MACS2 calls broad peaks by default; --narrow_peak selects narrow peaks. The default consensus set is the union of peaks across samples, so a peak need not occur in every sample. Increasing --min_reps_consensus requires greater replicate support.[5]
PCA and clustering show how similar the samples are. The pipeline uses DESeq2 to generate these plots. Identifying significantly different accessibility between treatment and control requires a statistical comparison based on the experimental groups.[5]

title: nf-core/atacseq: Mapping Accessible Chromatin with “Molecular Scissors”
text:
5. What Does nf-core/atacseq Produce?
The experiment tags accessible DNA; the pipeline analyzes where those tags occur.
Version 2.1.2 organizes read QC, adapter trimming, alignment, filtering, peak calling, and reporting into a Nextflow workflow, with containers managing software dependencies.[1]
A peak is a genomic interval with significant enrichment of sequencing signal.
Three questions provide a useful starting point for reading the results:[5]







Question
Relevant outputs




Is the data quality sufficient for further analysis?
MultiQC, ataqv, and associated QC metrics


Where are the accessibility signals?
MACS2 peaks and bigWig tracks


Can samples be compared across the same regions?
Consensus peaks, read count matrices, PCA, and clustering



Consensus peaks combine the individual peak sets into shared genomic intervals for comparison.[5]

title: nf-core/atacseq: Mapping Accessible Chromatin with “Molecular Scissors”
section: 6. What Comes After Finding Accessible Regions?
text:
6. What Comes After Finding Accessible Regions?
ATAC-seq adds another perspective to genome analysis: how cells make DNA accessible and organize it into chromatin.
nf-core/atacseq provides a reusable workflow for analyzing these signals. The next step is to connect accessible regions with gene expression and experimental conditions, developing biological explanations that can be tested.

title: Small Mistakes, Big Consequences: Notes on Common Errors in Bioinformatics
text:
6 min read
Most bioinformatics errors are not exotic. They are an index that starts at the wrong number, a genome build nobody wrote down, or a stray space in a shell command. They are easy to make, hard to spot, and often fail silently: the pipeline finishes and the output looks reasonable.

title: Small Mistakes, Big Consequences: Notes on Common Errors in Bioinformatics
section: 1. Counting Is Harder Than It Looks
text:
1. Counting Is Harder Than It Looks
Coordinate systems differ between file formats. BED intervals are 0-based and half-open, while GTF and GFF are 1-based and closed. The first base of a chromosome is 0 in BED and 1 in GTF. Converting between them without adjusting the start position shifts every feature by one base, which is enough to change a codon or miss a splice site.
Programming languages use different index origins. Python counts from 0; R counts from 1. Code ported from one language to the other can run without errors and still return the neighbouring element.
Chromosome names should not be sorted as plain text. A plain text sort places chr10 before chr2, breaking the usual numeric order. Use a natural sort to obtain chr1, chr2, …, chr10; for interval files such as BED, also sort by start coordinate within each chromosome.

Good practice: When a coordinate crosses a format or language boundary, check one known feature by hand, such as the start of a well-studied gene, before trusting the conversion.

title: Small Mistakes, Big Consequences: Notes on Common Errors in Bioinformatics
section: 2. The Data Do Not Match What You Think
text:
2. The Data Do Not Match What You Think
Genome builds must stay consistent. Reads aligned to hg19 but viewed against hg38 annotation appear to fall outside exons. Every reference file, index and annotation must come from the same assembly and, ideally, the same release.
Strand matters. A feature on the minus strand must be reverse-complemented before its sequence is used. Forgetting this produces a valid-looking but wrong sequence.
Define how to handle reads that match multiple genes before counting. Genes can overlap or be nested. Without a rule for shared regions, features may be missed or reads counted twice.
Line endings are a hidden trap. Files saved on Windows end lines with \r\n; Unix tools expect \n. A missing newline at the end of the last line can also cause a simple loop to skip it. dos2unix and a quick tail check help.

Good practice: Record the genome build and annotation version in file names and in a project README.

title: Small Mistakes, Big Consequences: Notes on Common Errors in Bioinformatics
text:
3. Shell Errors
Deleting or overwriting by accident.

A stray space turns rm *.fasta into rm * .fasta, which deletes everything in the folder.
> replaces a file’s contents, while >> appends. Redirecting with > into ~/.bashrc erases the existing configuration.
rm * in the wrong directory is not reversible.

Letting the shell interpret characters meant for a program.

awk {print $2} fails because the shell expands $2 and the braces; write awk '{print $2}'.
grep > file.fasta redirects output instead of searching for headers; write grep '>' file.fasta.
find . -name *.txt may expand the wildcard before find sees it; quote the pattern.

Forgetting a default.

cut splits on tabs unless told otherwise; a CSV needs -d,.
mkdir needs -p to create nested directories.
rm needs -r for directories.
cat on a multi-gigabyte FASTQ floods the terminal; head or less -S is safer.
chmod 777 grants everyone full access; chmod u+x is usually all that is needed.


Good practice: Before deleting with a wildcard, run ls with the same pattern first. In Bash, set -o noclobber stops > from overwriting an existing file.

title: Small Mistakes, Big Consequences: Notes on Common Errors in Bioinformatics
text:
4. Process Mistakes Outlast Code Mistakes
Use established tools rather than reinventing the wheel. To read FASTQ, GenBank or BLAST output, prefer tested libraries such as Biopython, pysam or Bioconductor packages: they save effort and handle edge cases that custom parsers often miss. For single-cell RNA-seq, use Scanpy or Seurat for quality control, dimensionality reduction and clustering, and spend the time saved on the research question.
Test regular expressions against examples you know should and should not match.
Track versions of data and code. Analyses that silently use an outdated input are hard to reproduce. Git, Git LFS or a workflow manager makes the inputs explicit.
Document decisions and use appropriate statistics. A result that cannot be explained, or that depends on an unsuitable test or poor randomization, is not yet a finding.

title: Small Mistakes, Big Consequences: Notes on Common Errors in Bioinformatics
text:
5. Common Mistakes in Single-Cell Analysis
Treating cells as independent replicates in differential expression. When comparing conditions such as healthy and disease, each with several samples, a common approach is to pool all cells per condition and test at the cell level. Cells from the same sample are not independent, and thousands of cells make p-values artificially small, producing many false positives. Pseudobulk analysis is more reliable: aggregate counts per sample, then compare samples.
Over-interpreting UMAP. UMAP is a non-linear dimensionality reduction method; distances between points or clusters have no reliable quantitative meaning. Use it to visualize structure, not to judge how similar cell populations are.
Assuming batch correction is safe. Batch correction and data integration rely on assumptions, and over-correction can remove genuine biological signal. A benchmark of seven widely used methods found that many introduce measurable artifacts; only Harmony performed consistently well, and it was the only method the authors recommended for scRNA-seq batch correction.Antonsson & Melsted, 2024

Good practice: Test differential expression at the sample level, treat UMAP as visualization only, and confirm that known biological differences survive batch correction.

title: Small Mistakes, Big Consequences: Notes on Common Errors in Bioinformatics
text:
A Short Checklist







Before you…
Check




Convert coordinates
0-based or 1-based? Half-open or closed?


Combine files
Same genome build and annotation release? Same chromosome naming (chr1 vs 1)?


Extract sequences
Which strand?


Run rm, > or mv
Correct directory? Pattern confirmed with ls?


Pass code to awk, grep or find
Quoted?


Compare conditions
Analysed at the sample level (pseudobulk)?


Share results
Inputs, versions and parameters documented?



None of these mistakes requires advanced knowledge to avoid. They require a moment of checking, which is cheaper than rerunning an analysis.

The main content of this post is based on my reading of Tommy Tang’s article “The Most Common Stupid Mistakes In Bioinformatics” on his blog, Chatomics. Please read the original for his full list and additional resources.
